title: Biomimicry: copying how living things solve their problems
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home today, with the materials listed. Fixes made. Leaves must be held by the stalk, because touching rubs off the wax (old or bruised leaves work less well, so pick a fresh one, and use an outer cabbage leaf if no chembu or lotus leaf can be found). The splash test counts wet spots on newspaper, because splash height is too hard to measure; the water must be 3 cm below the rim, and a beak that tumbles is dropped again from 20 cm. The ice test uses lidded cups and checks every 10 minutes. A bare cup's ice lasts about 20 to 40 minutes in strong sun. Wet cloth works less well on humid monsoon days. The Sock Walk works best from September to February and only on short weeds with a grown-up, because of snakes. Paperclip hooks must be small, and a grown-up bends them if the ends are sharp. Candle soot and the flame are grown-up steps, with a 2-minute cooling time. Cling film also holds partly by static, which the activity says honestly. Both games have rules for playing alone. Parents should know that the ice test needs about an hour, mostly waiting, so play the matching game in the shade meanwhile.

summary.text: Every plant and animal has problems to solve in their own life. A burdock plant must send their seeds far away, so their burrs carry hooks that catch on animal fur. A lotus leaf must stay clean in a muddy pond, so tiny waxy bumps make rain roll off and take the dirt with it. A kingfisher must dive without a splash that warns the fish, so their beak widens very slowly. These designs got better over many generations. People who studied them closely copied them, and made Velcro, self-cleaning paint and a quieter bullet train. Copying how a living thing solves a problem is called biomimicry.
summary.art: A child's notebook page: on the left a burr, a lotus leaf, a kingfisher, a gecko and a termite mound, and on the right, joined by dotted arrows, a Velcro strap, a raindrop rolling off a wall, a bullet train, a robot hand and a cool building.

intro.hook: Find a shoe or a bag with a Velcro strap. Look closely at its two sides. One side has tiny stiff hooks. The other side has soft loops. A plant was using hooks like these long before anyone made Velcro. Why would a plant need hooks?
intro.text: A burdock plant cannot walk. If their seeds just dropped to the ground, they would grow right under the parent plant. There they would have to share their parent's light, water and soil. So the burdock's seed heads, called burrs, are covered in stiff spines with tiny hooks at the tips. When a fox, a cow or a dog brushes past, the hooks catch in their fur. The animal carries the burr away, and the seeds fall off in new ground. Over many generations, burdock plants whose hooks gripped better spread further, so strong hooks became common. In 1941, a Swiss engineer called George de Mestral came home from a walk in the mountains with burrs all over his clothes and his dog. He looked at one under a microscope. He saw hundreds of tiny hooks caught in loops of fur and thread. He copied exactly that: one strip of hooks and one strip of loops. That became Velcro.
intro.art: A burdock plant with round prickly burrs, a dog walking past with burrs caught in their fur, and a round microscope view showing a burr's hooks caught in loops of fur.

outcomes: I can say what biomimicry is: learning how a living thing solves a problem in their own life, and using the same idea for a human problem.
I can explain why a burdock plant has hooked burrs, how Velcro copies them, and test what hooks hold on to best.
I can explain why a lotus leaf needs to stay clean, and how its tiny waxy bumps make water roll off and carry dirt away.
I can explain how a kingfisher dives with little splash and how a gecko clings to walls, and what engineers copied from each.
I can explain why termites need a cool, airy mound, and test which walls keep a model house coolest.
I can design, build and fairly test my own nature-inspired invention, record the results in a table and a bar chart, and improve it.

I can explain that these designs came about over many generations, because living things whose designs worked better left more young. I can also say what scientists agree on and what they still argue about.

terms.meaning: Learning how a plant or an animal solves a problem in their own life, and using the same idea to solve a human problem. 'Bio' means life. 'Mimic' means copy.
terms.example: Velcro copies the hooks that a burdock burr uses to catch on animal fur.
terms.art: A burr and a Velcro strap side by side, joined by a dotted arrow.

terms.meaning: A new thing, or a new way of doing something, that somebody thought up.
terms.example: The bicycle, the pressure cooker and Velcro are inventions.
terms.art: A light bulb above a child's head, and a pressure cooker, a bicycle and a Velcro strap below.

terms.meaning: A person who designs and builds things that solve problems, and tests them to see if they work.
terms.example: Engineers design bridges, trains, phones and water pumps.
terms.art: A woman engineer in a hard hat drawing a bridge, a small model bridge on her table.

terms.meaning: A plan for making something, drawn or written before you build it.
terms.example: A drawing of your invention with labels showing what each part does.
terms.art: A labelled pencil drawing of a backpack with arrows to its parts.

terms.meaning: A first, rough model of an invention, made to test if the idea works.
terms.example: A cardboard and paperclip fastener you make before a real one.
terms.art: A rough cardboard model held together with tape, next to a polished finished version.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the difference.
terms.example: Drop two dough shapes from the same height into the same bucket. Only the shape changes.
terms.art: Two identical buckets with two different dough shapes held at the same height above them.

terms.meaning: The seed head of some plants, covered in stiff spines with tiny hooks. The hooks catch in animal fur, so the animal carries the seeds to new ground.
terms.example: After a walk through dry weeds, your socks can be full of prickly seeds that hold on in the same way.
terms.art: A round burr covered in hooked spines, stuck to a dog's fur.

terms.meaning: The ways plants send their seeds away from the parent plant. Seeds that land far away have more light, water and space to grow.
terms.example: Burrs ride on animal fur, dandelion seeds fly on the wind, and coconuts float across the sea.
terms.art: A parent plant in the middle, with arrows to seeds travelling away: a burr on a dog, a fluffy seed in the wind, a coconut on a wave.

terms.meaning: A way of joining two things. One side has tiny stiff hooks. The other side has tiny soft loops. The hooks catch in the loops.
terms.example: Velcro on school shoes and bags is hook and loop.
terms.art: A zoom into Velcro: stiff hooks on one side catching soft loops on the other.

terms.meaning: The way some leaves keep themselves clean. Tiny waxy bumps make water roll off in balls, and the balls carry the dirt away.
terms.example: After rain, lotus and chembu (colocasia, also called arbi) leaves have silver balls of water rolling on them, and look spotless.
terms.art: A lotus leaf with shiny round water drops, one drop rolling and picking up dust.

terms.meaning: A smooth, slippery material that water does not soak into. Many leaves make a thin layer of it on their surface.
terms.example: Candle wax, and the shiny coat on a cabbage leaf.
terms.art: A candle and a cabbage leaf, both with water drops beading up on them.

terms.meaning: When a surface makes water stay in round drops instead of spreading or soaking in.
terms.example: A raincoat is water-repelling. A paper towel is not. It soaks water up.
terms.art: A drop sitting round on a raincoat next to a drop soaking into a paper towel.

terms.meaning: Shaped so that air or water can flow smoothly around it. A streamlined thing is usually pointed at the front and smooth all over.
terms.example: Fish, dolphins, kingfishers and racing cyclists' helmets are streamlined.
terms.art: A fish, a kingfisher and a bullet train lined up, all with the same pointed shape.

terms.meaning: The push of air or water against something moving through it. Drag slows things down.
terms.example: Put your hand out of a moving bus window. The air pushing it back is drag.
terms.art: A hand out of a bus window with air arrows pushing it back.

terms.meaning: A loud bang when a fast train comes out of a tunnel. The train squeezes the air ahead of it inside the tunnel, and the squeezed air bursts out of the far end.
terms.example: Houses near tunnels in Japan were shaken by tunnel booms from early bullet trains.
terms.art: A tunnel in a hill with a burst of sound lines coming out of the far end before the train.

terms.meaning: A small lizard that can run up walls and walk upside down on ceilings. The house gecko, the chhipkali, lives in many Indian homes.
terms.example: A gecko waiting for insects near the tube light.
terms.art: A house gecko upside down on a ceiling near a tube light.

terms.meaning: The tiny hairs on a gecko's toes. Each one splits into hundreds of even tinier tips. Say it 'SEE-tee'.
terms.example: One gecko has millions of setae on their toes.
terms.art: A zoom from a gecko's toe to rows of hairs, to one hair splitting into a brush of tiny tips.

terms.meaning: A tall tower of mud that termites build. Millions of termites live in tunnels under and inside it.
terms.example: In parts of south India, termite mounds taller than a child stand in fields and forests.
terms.art: A tall reddish termite mound in a dry field, taller than the child standing next to it.

terms.meaning: A thick layer that slows down heat getting in or out.
terms.example: A thick blanket keeps you warm. A thick mud wall keeps a hut cool in summer.
terms.art: A mud hut with thick walls, sun arrows bouncing off and only small arrows getting in.

terms.meaning: The slow change of living things over many, many generations. Young ones differ a little from their parents. Those whose differences help them live and have young pass those features on, so the features spread.
terms.example: Over many generations, burdock burrs with better hooks were carried further, so burdock plants today have strong hooks.
terms.art: A row of burrs from left to right, each with slightly better hooks, under a long arrow labelled 'millions of years'.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: A leaf, a drop of water and your hand are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a lotus leaf to a waxy bump, to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: An official paper from the government. It says an invention belongs to its inventor for some years, so nobody else can copy it and sell it.
terms.example: George de Mestral applied for a patent for Velcro in 1951.
terms.art: An old official document with a stamp and a drawing of hooks and loops.

explanations.definition: Biomimicry means studying how a plant or an animal solves a problem in their own life, and using the same idea to solve a human problem. People copy the idea, not the whole living thing.
explanations.description: Every living thing has problems in their own life. A plant must spread their seeds and keep their leaves clean. An animal must catch food, grip a branch or keep their home cool. Over many generations, living things have worked out designs that solve these problems. A person who wants to copy one must first understand it. What problem does the living thing have? How exactly does its design solve it? Only then can the same idea be built from materials people can make. An American scientist, Otto Schmitt, used the word 'biomimetics' for this in the 1950s. In 1997, an American nature writer, Janine Benyus, wrote a book called 'Biomimicry'. It made the word famous around the world.
examples: A burdock burr's hooks carry its seeds away on animal fur. Velcro copies them to fasten shoes.
A kingfisher's beak lets them dive without warning the fish. A bullet train's nose copies it to leave tunnels quietly.
A lotus leaf's waxy bumps keep it clean in a muddy pond. Self-cleaning paint copies them.
explanations.art: Three panels: a burr becoming Velcro, a kingfisher becoming a train, a lotus leaf becoming a clean painted wall.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what biomimicry means.

explanations.concept: Why a burdock burr has hooks, and how Velcro copied them
explanations.definition: A burdock burr is covered in stiff spines with tiny hooks. The hooks catch in animal fur, so animals carry the seeds to new ground. Velcro copies this: one strip has hooks and the other has loops.
explanations.description: A burdock plant stays rooted in one place all their life. Their seeds need to grow somewhere else. Under the parent plant, they would have to share light, water and soil with their parent, and with each other. The burdock's answer is the burr, a ball of seeds covered in hooked spines. When an animal brushes past, the hooks catch in their fur. The burr may ride a long way before it is scratched off or falls. Then its seeds can grow in new ground, with less crowding. Burdock plants whose hooks gripped well spread further, so over many generations strong hooks became the rule. In 1941, George de Mestral, a Swiss engineer, looked at burrs from his dog's fur under a microscope. He saw the hooks caught in loops of fur. He wanted two strips of cloth that would join in the same way. Making it work took about ten years. Cotton loops wore out fast, but nylon, a strong plastic thread, worked well. He applied for a patent in 1951. He named his fastener Velcro, from two French words: 'velours', meaning velvet, and 'crochet', meaning hook.
examples: Velcro straps on school shoes, bags and blood pressure cuffs.
Astronauts used Velcro to stop things floating away inside their spacecraft.
A burr catches on a woollen sock but slides off a smooth raincoat, because the raincoat has no loops for its hooks.
explanations.art: A burr under a microscope showing curled hooks, next to Velcro under a microscope showing hooks and loops.
explanations.context: Have you ever come home with prickly seeds stuck to your socks? This card explains why plants make them, and how they gave us Velcro.

explanations.concept: Why a lotus leaf stays clean
explanations.definition: A lotus leaf is covered in tiny bumps, and the bumps are coated in even tinier bits of wax. Water cannot spread on it, so it makes balls that roll off and carry dirt away. Scientists call this the lotus effect.
explanations.description: A lotus grows in muddy ponds, and their big round leaves lie open to the sky. Dust, splashes of mud and the spores of fungi land on them all the time. Dirt on a leaf blocks the sunlight it needs to make its food. Spores and germs left on a leaf can make it sick. Yet lotus leaves look clean. In the 1970s, a German plant scientist called Wilhelm Barthlott looked at leaves with a very powerful microscope, called a scanning electron microscope. The lotus leaf was not smooth at all. It was covered in tiny bumps, and the bumps were coated with even tinier bits of wax. A water drop rests only on the tips of the bumps, with air underneath. So it stays round and rolls off at the smallest tilt. Dirt grips the water better than it grips the waxy tips, so each rolling drop picks up dirt and carries it away. Every shower of rain washes the leaf. Over many generations, lotus plants whose leaves stayed cleaner grew better and left more seeds. Barthlott and Christoph Neinhuis described the lotus effect in 1997. In the late 1990s, a paint company made an outside wall paint with the same kind of tiny bumps, so that rain washes the wall clean.
examples: Chembu (colocasia, also called arbi) leaves, nasturtium leaves and cabbage leaves show the same effect.
Self-cleaning paint, glass and cloth copy the lotus effect.
Touching a lotus leaf rubs off its wax. Then that spot gets wet like an ordinary leaf.
explanations.art: A zoom: a lotus leaf, then a close-up of bumps like tiny hills with frosty wax, then a round water drop sitting on the tips with air below.
explanations.context: Lotus leaves grow in muddy ponds, yet they always look clean. This card explains why the plant needs clean leaves, and the surprising way the plant keeps them clean.

explanations.concept: Deep down: why water makes balls
explanations.definition: Water is made of tiny particles called molecules. Water molecules pull on each other strongly. On a waxy, bumpy surface, they pull on each other far more than on the surface. So the water pulls itself into a ball.
explanations.description: Zoom into a drop of water, far past anything a microscope can show. It is made of countless water molecules, each one built from three atoms. Every molecule tugs on the ones around it. At the edge of a drop, all that tugging pulls the water into a round shape, like a stretched skin. Scientists call this surface tension. On paper, the paper pulls the water too, so it spreads and soaks in. Wax hardly pulls on water at all. On the lotus, the drop also rests mostly on air between the bumps. Air does not pull the water either. So the water's own pull wins, and the drop becomes almost a perfect ball. The pull between molecules, and between wax and water, is an electric pull between their atoms. It is the same kind of force that gives us friction and holds a gecko on a wall.
examples: A drop on a candle stays round. A drop on a tissue spreads and soaks in.
Water striders, small insects, stand on a pond because surface tension holds them up.
explanations.art: A water drop cut open to show tiny balls (molecules) holding hands, sitting on wax bumps with air pockets underneath.
explanations.context: Why does water make a ball on a lotus leaf but soak into paper? This card zooms in to the tiny molecules of water to find out.

explanations.concept: The kingfisher and the bullet train
explanations.definition: A kingfisher must dive from air into water fast, without a big splash that warns the fish. Their long beak widens very slowly, so it parts the water gently. Engineers copied that shape for the nose of a Japanese bullet train, so it left tunnels without a loud boom.
explanations.description: A kingfisher lives by catching small fish. The bird sits still on a branch above the water, watching. When they see a fish, they dive. Water is about 800 times heavier than the same amount of air, so it is hard to push aside. A blunt head would slap the water, slow the bird down and send out ripples that warn the fish. The kingfisher's beak is long and narrow, and it widens slowly towards the head. So it pushes the water aside a little at a time, and the bird slips in with only a small splash. Over many generations, kingfishers that dived more smoothly caught more fish and raised more chicks. Japan's bullet trains, called Shinkansen, had a problem like this. When a fast train rushed into a tunnel, it squeezed the air ahead of it. The squeezed air burst out of the far end with a boom that shook nearby houses. Eiji Nakatsu, an engineer and a birdwatcher, saw that the train and the kingfisher had the same problem. Each moves fast into a place where the water or air cannot easily get out of the way. His team tested many nose shapes. The shape most like a kingfisher's beak worked best. The 500 Series train, which began running in 1997, had a long beak-shaped nose. It was quieter in tunnels, and it used less electricity. Nakatsu has said that he also learned from owl feathers, to make the arm on the train's roof quieter.
examples: A kingfisher dives into a pond and leaves only a small ring on the water.
A pointed dough shape dropped into a bucket splashes far less than a flat one.
India's first bullet train line, between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, is being built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.
explanations.art: A kingfisher diving into water with a tiny splash, above a white bullet train with a long beak-shaped nose coming out of a tunnel quietly.
explanations.context: The common kingfisher lives by ponds and canals across India and Japan. This card shows how their beak solves their own problem, and how it helped make a bullet train quieter.

explanations.concept: The same shape, again and again
explanations.definition: Animals that are not close relatives often end up with the same shape, because they face the same problem. Scientists call this convergent evolution. Engineers who test shapes often reach the same answer too.
explanations.description: Sharks are fish. Dolphins are mammals, like us. Ichthyosaurs were reptiles that lived in the sea in the time of the dinosaurs. They are not close relatives at all. Yet all three have the same shape: a pointed nose, a smooth body and a strong tail. Why? Because water pushes back in the same way on every swimmer. A fast swimmer with a blunt nose wastes its energy pushing water. Over millions of years, the fast, pointed ones caught more food and left more young. Engineers testing train noses in the 1990s did not wait millions of years. They tested shapes in days. But they arrived at the same answer as the kingfisher. Nature and engineers are solving the same problems, under the same rules.
examples: Penguins, seals and fish all have smooth, pointed bodies for swimming.
Bats, birds and insects all grew wings, in three different ways.
Racing cyclists and diving birds both tuck into a pointed shape.
explanations.art: A shark, a dolphin and an ichthyosaur swimming in a row, all the same shape, with a bullet train nose beside them.
explanations.context: A shark, a dolphin and a train nose look alike. This card explains why very different things end up with the same shape.

explanations.concept: How a gecko sticks to a wall
explanations.description: A house gecko hunts insects on walls, windows and ceilings, often near a light at night. They must run up smooth glass, hang upside down and not fall. Its feet have no glue and no suckers. Each toe has rows of tiny hairs called setae. Each hair splits into hundreds of even tinier tips. The tips are so small and bendy that they get extremely close to the wall, even into its tiny dips. When atoms get that close, they pull on each other very slightly. One tip's pull is tiny. But a gecko has millions of hairs and hundreds of millions of tips. All those tiny pulls add up. Geckos whose feet gripped better caught more insects and escaped more snakes, so over many generations their feet became the grippers we see today. Scientists agree on this much. They argue about one part: does water help?
examples: A house gecko walks upside down on the ceiling near the tube light.
Geckos find it hard to grip Teflon, the very slippery coating on non-stick pans.

perspectives.who: Kellar Autumn and his team, in the USA, in 2000 and 2002
perspectives.explanation: They measured the pull of a single gecko hair for the first time. Then they tested geckos on surfaces that water sticks to and surfaces water rolls off. Geckos gripped both about the same. So they said the grip comes from the pull between atoms, called van der Waals forces, not from water.

perspectives.who: Gerrit Huber and others, in Germany, in 2005
perspectives.explanation: They found single gecko hair tips grip harder when the air is damp. A very thin film of water from the air may help the tips hold on. So water helps too.
The pull between atoms does most of the work. A thin film of water can add to it on damp days. How much each matters is still being studied.

explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a gecko on a window, a toe with lines of ridges, rows of tiny hairs, and one hair splitting into a brush of tips touching the glass.
explanations.context: A gecko can hang from a ceiling by one toe, with no glue. This card explains how their tiny hairs grip, and what scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: How a gecko lets go, and the inventions it inspired
explanations.definition: A gecko lets go by peeling their toes up from the tip, like peeling sticky tape. Engineers have copied gecko hairs to make dry tape and robot grippers that need no glue.
explanations.description: Holding on is only half of the gecko's problem. A gecko running up a wall must stick and unstick each foot many times every second. If you pull tape straight off a wall, it holds hard. If you peel it from one corner, it comes off easily. Gecko toes peel from the tip, a few hairs at a time. So letting go takes almost no effort. Gecko feet also stay clean. Dirt falls off the tiny tips as the gecko walks. In 2003, a team in Manchester, England, led by Andre Geim made a small patch of 'gecko tape' from plastic hairs. At Stanford University in the USA, engineers built a climbing robot called Stickybot in 2006. NASA engineers have built gecko-style grippers to grab things in space, where glue and suckers do not work well.
examples: Peel sticky tape from a corner and it comes away easily. Pull it straight and it holds.
Gecko-style grippers can pick up a smooth glass plate and let it go with no mark left behind.
explanations.art: A gecko toe curling up from the tip like peeling tape, next to a small robot with gecko-like pads climbing a glass wall.
explanations.context: Sticking is easy. Unsticking quickly is the hard part. This card shows how geckos let go, and what engineers have made from their feet.

explanations.description: Termites are small insects that live in huge families, sometimes of millions. Some kinds build mounds taller than a grown-up. Deep inside, many kinds grow a fungus garden. The fungus breaks down the dry plants the termites bring in, and turns them into food the termites can eat. The garden and the termites need air that stays fresh, damp and not too hot. Millions of termites and their fungus breathe out a lot of carbon dioxide, which must get out. Outside, the sun may be baking. Termites whose mounds kept the nest fresh and steady raised more young, so over very many generations their way of building spread. Two things are agreed. First, the thick earth walls slow down the heat, so the inside changes temperature much less than the outside. Second, air moves through tiny holes in the walls. How the air is moved is the part scientists have changed their minds about.
examples: In parts of south India, the termite Odontotermes obesus builds mounds taller than a child.
Inside a mound on a hot afternoon, it is far cooler than the ground in the sun.

perspectives.who: The old idea, from Martin Lüscher, a Swiss scientist, in 1961
perspectives.explanation: The termites' own warmth heats the air, which rises up a central chimney and draws fresh air in, like a fire drawing air up a chimney.

perspectives.who: Hunter King, Samuel Ocko and L. Mahadevan, scientists at Harvard University, in 2015
perspectives.explanation: They put tiny sensors into real mounds near Bengaluru. They found the mound breathes with the day and night. In the day, the thin outer walls warm faster than the middle, and air moves one way. At night, the walls cool faster, and air moves the other way.

perspectives.who: J. Scott Turner, an American scientist who studied African mounds
perspectives.explanation: Wind gusting over the mound also pushes and pulls the air inside. Different kinds of mound may work in different ways. The full story is still being worked out.

explanations.art: A cut-away termite mound with red arrows of air moving one way in the daytime sun, and blue arrows moving the other way under a night sky.
explanations.context: A termite mound stays cool inside on a burning hot day, with no fans. This card shows how, and how scientists changed their minds about it.

explanations.definition: Some architects design buildings with thick walls, and air channels that let cool night air flush through. These ideas were inspired by termite mounds. They keep buildings cooler with less air conditioning.
explanations.description: In 1996, the Eastgate Centre opened in Harare, the capital city of Zimbabwe in Africa. Its architect, Mick Pearce, studied termite mounds. The building has thick concrete walls and floors that soak up heat slowly in the day. At night, fans pull cool outside air through hollow spaces in the floors, and warm air leaves through chimneys on the roof. Its designers reported that it uses much less energy for cooling than similar buildings. The building was based on the old chimney idea of how mounds work. Scientists later found mounds work differently. The building still works well. So a copy can be useful even when the original is not fully understood. In India, old houses with thick mud walls, small windows and courtyards also stay cool in the heat.
examples: Thick mud walls of village houses keep rooms cool in summer.
A clay water pot (a matka or kooja), keeps water cool because water seeps through its clay and evaporates from the outside, and that carries heat away.
explanations.art: A tall building with chimneys on its roof next to a termite mound with the same shape, cool blue arrows flowing through both at night.
explanations.context: Termites keep their homes cool without electricity. This card is about a building in Africa that copied them.

explanations.concept: Copy how it works, not how it looks
explanations.definition: Good biomimicry copies how something works, not just how it looks. A machine that only looks like an animal usually does not work like one.
explanations.description: Around the year 1500, Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian artist and inventor, drew flying machines with flapping wings like a bird's. None of them flew. Copying the look of flapping was not enough. Four hundred years later, people studied how birds really fly. Otto Lilienthal, a German engineer, studied storks and wrote a book about bird flight in 1889. He made gliders that really flew. Wilbur and Orville Wright, two brothers in the USA, watched birds twist the tips of their wings to balance. They copied that twist, not the flapping. In 1903 they made the first powered aeroplane flight. Here in India, the Lotus Temple in Delhi copies the look of a lotus flower. It is beautiful, but its walls do not clean themselves. Self-cleaning paint looks nothing like a lotus, but it copies the lotus leaf's design.
examples: The bullet train's nose does not have feathers or eyes. It copies only the beak's slow widening.
Velcro does not look like a burr. It copies only the hooks.
explanations.art: Two panels: Leonardo's flapping machine with a red cross, and the Wright brothers' plane with twisted wingtips and a tick.
explanations.context: This card is about the biggest lesson for inventors who copy nature: copy how it works, not how it looks.

explanations.definition: Nature's designs come about through evolution. Over many generations, living things whose features solve their problems better leave more young. So those features spread.
explanations.description: The burdock's hooks were not made in one go. They got better along a very long line of burdock plants. Young plants differ a little from their parents, the way you differ from yours. Long ago, some burdock plants had burrs that gripped fur slightly better. Their burrs were carried further, so more of their seeds grew. Their young had good hooks too, because living things pass their features on. Over many generations, strong hooks became common. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace explained this in 1858. Scientists call it evolution by natural selection. Life on Earth began about 3.8 billion years ago. Every plant and animal alive today comes from a long line of living things that solved the problems of their lives well enough to have young. Janine Benyus says nature has been testing its designs for 3.8 billion years. Engineers are learning to read the results.
examples: Kingfishers whose beaks made less splash caught more fish, and raised more chicks.
Geckos that gripped better escaped from snakes, and lived to lay eggs.
explanations.art: A long timeline from tiny cells 3.8 billion years ago to a burr, a kingfisher and a gecko today, with a child at the end holding a notebook.
explanations.context: Who designed the burr's hooks and the gecko's toes? This card explains where nature's designs come from.

explanations.description: People who love biomimicry often say nature's designs are the best. Others say that is not quite right. Both sides have good points.
examples: Your eye has a blind spot, where the nerve leaves it. An octopus eye is built the other way round and has no blind spot.
Bacteria have a tiny spinning motor to swim, but no animal grew a wheel to roll on.

perspectives.who: Janine Benyus and many people who work in biomimicry
perspectives.explanation: Nature has tested its designs for billions of years. Nature's designs are also made from water, sunlight and simple materials, at ordinary temperatures, and they rot away safely when they are finished. We should learn from that.
Evolution makes things good enough to survive, not perfect. It can only change what is already there, a little at a time. So living things carry old mistakes, like the blind spot in your eye.
People have made things nature never made: wheels that roll, metal tools, fire for cooking, rockets. The best ideas often mix nature's designs with human ones.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a kingfisher and a gecko on one side, and a wheel, a rocket and a flame on the other.
explanations.context: Many people say nature is the greatest designer. This card asks whether that is true, and gives three different views.

explanations.description: An inventor who copies a burr can get a patent. A patent is an official paper that says nobody else may copy and sell the invention for some years. But nobody pays the burr. And sometimes the 'new' idea was known by people for hundreds of years. In 1995, two scientists in the USA got a patent for using turmeric to heal wounds. Families in India had used it for centuries. India's science council, the CSIR, showed the judges very old Indian books that described it. In 1997, the patent was cancelled.
examples: Haldi on a cut is an old Indian home remedy.
Jagadish Chandra Bose, the Indian scientist, did not want to make money from his radio research, and shared it freely. Friends persuaded him to take just one patent, in the USA in 1904.

perspectives.explanation: Patents reward people for years of hard work. George de Mestral spent about ten years making Velcro work. Without patents, fewer people would try.

perspectives.who: Many people in India and other countries
perspectives.explanation: Knowledge that communities have had for centuries should not be taken and owned by one company. In 2001, India started a huge library of traditional knowledge, so it cannot be patented by others.
Ideas copied from nature, and ideas that help people, should be free for everyone.

explanations.art: A burr, a lotus and a turmeric root sitting in a courtroom's witness box, while people argue over a paper with a big stamp.
explanations.context: When someone copies a plant's idea, who should own it? This card is about patents, turmeric and fairness.

explanations.description: Biomimicry is still young. Scientists are trying many new ideas, and most are not yet in our homes. The pitcher plant grows where the soil has little food in it for plants. They get extra food by catching insects. Pitcher plants whose rims trapped more insects grew better and made more seeds, so over many generations the slippery rim spread. The rim of their pitcher is so slippery when wet that insects slide in and cannot climb out. India's own pitcher plant grows in the hills of Meghalaya. In 2011, a team led by Joanna Aizenberg at Harvard University made a coating that copies the slippery rim. Almost nothing sticks to it, not even oil. In the Namib Desert in Africa, almost no rain falls, but fog blows in from the sea. A beetle there stands with their back to the foggy wind. Water from the fog gathers on bumps on their back and runs down to their mouth. Over many generations, beetles that caught more fog water survived the dry times better. Scientists described it in 2001, and others are testing fog-catching surfaces like it. Some scientists are trying to build an 'artificial leaf' that makes fuel from sunlight and water, as a plant makes food. Nobody yet knows which of these will work well enough to use every day.
examples: A ketchup or honey bottle that empties completely, with nothing stuck to the sides.
Nets that catch drinking water from fog on dry hills.
explanations.art: A pitcher plant with an ant sliding into their pitcher, a desert beetle with a fog drop on their back, and a green artificial leaf making bubbles in sunlight.
explanations.context: Velcro and lotus paint are old now. This card is about new copies of nature that scientists are still testing.

agreed.text: Many useful inventions copy designs that plants and animals use to solve their own problems.
agreed.evidence: George de Mestral told how burrs from his walk gave him the idea for Velcro. Eiji Nakatsu has described how the kingfisher shaped the 500 Series train nose.

agreed.text: Lotus leaves stay clean because they are covered in tiny waxy bumps.
agreed.evidence: Powerful microscopes show the bumps and the wax. You can see drops roll off and carry dust away. If you rub the wax off, that spot gets wet.

agreed.text: Geckos stick to walls without glue or suckers, using millions of tiny hairs.
agreed.evidence: Gecko feet leave no glue behind. Scientists have measured the pull of a single hair. Geckos grip badly on Teflon, a coating that atoms hardly pull on.

agreed.text: A pointed, streamlined shape moves through air and water with less drag than a blunt one.
agreed.evidence: Engineers measure this with models in water tanks and wind tunnels. You can see it at home: a pointed dough shape splashes far less than a flat one.

agreed.text: Nature's designs come from evolution over very long times.
agreed.evidence: Fossils, the stony remains of ancient life, show living things slowly changing. DNA, the instructions inside every cell, shows how living things are related.

challenging.claim: NASA, the American space agency, invented Velcro.
challenging.who: A popular story, often heard in schools
challenging.for: Astronauts used Velcro in the 1960s, in the Apollo spacecraft that went to the Moon. It held their pens and food packets in place, so they did not float away.
challenging.against: George de Mestral invented Velcro. He applied for his patent in 1951, years before NASA started using it. NASA made Velcro famous, but did not invent it.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story of who invented Velcro.

challenging.claim: The smoother and shinier a surface, the cleaner it stays.
challenging.who: A common belief. Most of us think this without noticing.
challenging.for: Smooth glass and polished steel are easy to wipe clean.
challenging.against: The lotus leaf stays clean because it is bumpy, not smooth. On a smooth surface, water drops stick and leave dirty marks when they dry. On the bumpy, waxy lotus, drops roll off and take the dirt with them.
challenging.context: This card is about what makes a surface stay clean.

challenging.claim: To copy nature, make your machine look like the animal.
challenging.who: Many early inventors, including some who tried to fly
challenging.for: Birds fly by flapping, so a flying machine should flap too.
challenging.against: Flapping machines did not fly. The Wright brothers copied a design instead: birds twist their wingtips to balance. Good biomimicry copies how a thing works, not what it looks like.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many inventors made when they copied birds.

challenging.claim: The Eastgate Centre in Zimbabwe cools itself exactly the way a termite mound does.
challenging.who: Many books and websites about biomimicry
challenging.for: Its architect, Mick Pearce, studied termite mounds. The building has thick walls, air channels and chimneys, and uses little energy for cooling.
challenging.against: It was based on the old chimney idea of how mounds work. Scientists later found real mounds breathe with day and night, and with the wind. The building also uses fans. It was inspired by termites, but it does not work quite like a mound.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous building in Africa that is said to copy termite mounds.

challenging.claim: A gecko sticks with sticky glue or tiny suction cups.
challenging.who: A common guess, and an idea some scientists once had
challenging.for: Some animals, like octopuses, really do use suckers. And sticky things usually have glue.
challenging.against: Gecko feet leave no glue. Experiments showed geckos still cling when the air is pumped away, so it is not suction. The grip comes from hundreds of millions of tiny hair tips getting extremely close to the wall.
challenging.context: This card is about old guesses for how geckos cling to walls and ceilings.

challenging.claim: A car shaped like a boxfish proved that fish shapes are the best for cars.
challenging.who: The company Mercedes-Benz, with its boxfish concept car in 2005
challenging.for: The boxfish is a small reef fish that looks like a box. The car copied their shape, and in tests it slipped through the air very easily.
challenging.against: Later, scientists studied real boxfish. They found the boxfish's shape helps it turn quickly, more than it helps it swim straight with little drag. The car never went on sale. Copying a living thing needs a careful look at what its shape is really for.
challenging.context: This card is about a car that copied a fish, and what scientists later found out about the fish.

big_questions.q: A burdock plant's hooks gave us Velcro. Should the plant get any credit? Who should own an idea that came from nature?
big_questions.hint: Think about George de Mestral's ten years of work. Then think about the burdock plants' many generations.

big_questions.q: Is a bullet train natural or man-made? Where exactly would you draw the line?
big_questions.hint: The train is made by people. People are made by nature. The nose was copied from a bird.

big_questions.q: Why does a lotus leaf stay clean, when a shiny steel plate does not?
big_questions.hint: Look at a lotus or chembu leaf with a magnifying glass. Is it really smooth?

big_questions.q: Sharks, dolphins and kingfishers are not close relatives. Why do they share the same pointed shape?
big_questions.hint: What problem do they all have to solve?

big_questions.q: How can something as tiny as the pull between atoms hold up a whole gecko?
big_questions.hint: Think about one strand of thread, and then a thick rope made of millions of strands.

big_questions.q: If nature has been testing designs for 3.8 billion years, does that make nature wise?
big_questions.hint: Is cleverness only the kind that happens in a head? What kind of cleverness does a river have when it finds the easiest way downhill?

big_questions.q: Plants and animals are dying out faster than ever because of people. What designs might we lose before we even see them?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have named less than a quarter of the kinds of living things on Earth, by many estimates.

big_questions.q: Is it fair to copy a living thing's design and not give anything back to it?
big_questions.hint: What could people do for lotus ponds, geckos and termites, in return?

big_questions.q: The Bhagavad Gita says a wise person is like a lotus leaf in water. What could that mean?
big_questions.hint: The leaf lives on the pond, yet the water does not wet it.

big_questions.q: Nature never grew a wheel to roll on. But people did. Are there things only people can invent?
big_questions.hint: Bacteria have a tiny spinning motor. Is that a kind of wheel?

big_questions.q: Termite mounds have no fans and no electricity, and stay cool. What could our homes learn from them?
big_questions.hint: Think about thick walls, shade, and when the air outside is coolest.

story.title: The Quietest Splash
story.note: Eiji Nakatsu, the tunnel boom, his birdwatching, the kingfisher idea, the owl feathers and the 500 Series train of 1997 are real. The kingfisher who tells the story, Mei, her baby brother and her letters are made up.
text: I am a kingfisher. I am the size of a sparrow. My back is the blue of a gas flame, and my front is the orange of a ripe mango. My kind lives by slow rivers and ponds in many countries. We live in England, all across India, and in Japan, where I live. This is the story of my river, of the hole in the mountain beside it, and of a man who sat very still.

My river runs past rice fields and a bamboo grove, and then under a mountain. The people dug a long hole through the mountain. They call it a tunnel. Through it run the white trains, some of the fastest trains in the world. People call them bullet trains.

I did not mind the trains going in. They went in with a rush and a hiss. What I minded was the other end. A moment after a train went in, the far side of the mountain coughed. BOOM. It was a sound like a giant slamming a door. The herons in the rice fields jumped into the air. The windows of the houses rattled. And in the house by the bamboo, a baby began to cry. He cried every time a train went through, from morning until night.

The baby's sister was called Mei. She was nine. She often sat on the riverbank with a notebook, drawing me. She was not very good at sitting still, so I usually flew off before she finished. But I liked her. She wrote letters too. I saw her post them in the red box by the road. Later I heard her mother say that Mei had written to the train company. 'Please make your train quieter,' she had written. 'My brother cannot sleep.'

I knew why the mountain boomed. Birds understand air. When a train rushed into the tunnel, it pushed the air in front of it, like a hand pushing water along a narrow drain. The air had nowhere to go. It squeezed tighter and tighter, and it raced ahead of the train. At the far end, it burst out into the open. BOOM. The faster the trains went, the louder the boom became. And every year the trains went faster.

One spring a man began to come to my river. He came on his days off. He had binoculars, a notebook and a flask of tea. He sat on a rock under the willow for hours and hours, and he did not move. Most people walk along a river talking and pointing, and every bird flies away. This man watched. People who watch birds properly learn to be part of the riverbank.
So I fished as usual. I sat on my branch above the water, as still as he was. I saw a silver flick below. I dropped.

This is how I fish. I fall from the thin, soft air into the thick, heavy water, as fast as I can. Water is hard to push. If I hit it flat, it would slap me like a wall, and the fish would see the splash and dart away. But my beak is long and straight and sharp. From its tip, it gets wider very slowly, and then my head gets wider slowly, and then my body. So I do not push the water all at once. I push it aside a little at a time, from the tip backwards. I went in with a tiny sound, ploop. I left a ring on the water no bigger than a coin. I came out with a fish.

The man stood up on his rock. He nearly dropped his tea. He began to write in his notebook very fast. I heard him say something to himself. 'From thin air into thick water,' he said. 'From open air into a tight tunnel. It is the same problem.'

I did not understand his words then. I only noticed he was happy. That night, an owl hunted over the rice fields. Owls fly with almost no sound, because the edges of their feathers are soft and fringed. The man was there in the dark too, listening to nothing.
Then he stopped coming for a long time. The trains still boomed. Mei's brother still cried. Mei stopped writing letters and started drawing trains instead. Her trains had long, pointed faces.
Three summers went by. I raised two families of chicks in my burrow in the riverbank. I taught them to sit still, to watch, and to drop.

Then one morning a new train came. It was grey and blue, and it had the longest nose I had ever seen. The nose did not end in a round face like the old trains. It stretched out long and thin, and it widened very slowly, all the way back to the windows. It looked like my beak. It slid into the tunnel with a long, soft hiss.
I waited on my branch for the far side of the mountain to cough. The herons waited. The house by the bamboo waited.
Nothing came. Only a hush, like wind in the bamboo.

The door of the house opened, and Mei came out with her baby brother in her arms. He was fast asleep. She stood looking at the mountain for a long time. Then she looked at the river, at my branch, at me.

Later that day she sat on the bank and drew in her notebook again. She drew the new train. Next to it, she drew me, diving. She was careful to make the beak and the nose exactly the same shape. For once, I sat still until she had finished.

People tell this story now in many countries. They say that a train copied a kingfisher. I am not sure it is quite like that. The water taught my family its lesson over millions of years. The air taught the man the same lesson in a few. We were both listening to the same teacher. I just heard it first.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the train's boom and the kingfisher's splash are the same problem. A fast thing pushes into something that cannot easily get out of its way: water for the bird, the air inside a tunnel for the train. Hitting it with a blunt front shoves it all at once, which makes a slap or a boom. A long, slowly widening front pushes it aside a little at a time. The engineer did not copy the bird's look. He copied how the beak works. The story also quietly asks who teaches whom, and whether 'natural' and 'man-made' are really separate.
ask: Why did the tunnel boom when the old trains came out?
How does the kingfisher dive without a big splash? What is special about the shape of their beak?
The man said, 'It is the same problem.' What did he mean?
Why do you think the man sat so still for so long?
At the end, the kingfisher says they were both listening to the same teacher. Who or what was the teacher?

A burst of sound lines coming out of the far end of the tunnel, herons jumping up from rice fields, a baby crying in a house by bamboo.
A man with binoculars sitting very still on a rock under a willow, a flask of tea beside him.
The kingfisher diving into the water with only a tiny ring of ripples.
A long-nosed grey and blue train sliding silently into the tunnel, and a girl on the riverbank drawing the train and the bird side by side.

games.title: Nature's Idea Match
games.context: This is a matching card game about biomimicry. Each green card is a living thing, with the problem its design solves in its own life. Each orange card is an invention that copied that design. You find the pairs and explain them.

printables.title: 10 green NATURE cards to cut out
items: Burdock burr: hooked spines that catch on fur, so animals carry its seeds away
Lotus leaf: tiny waxy bumps that make rain roll off and wash the leaf clean
Kingfisher: a long beak that widens slowly, so they dive without warning the fish
Owl: soft, fringed feather edges, so they fly almost silently to their prey
Gecko: millions of tiny toe hairs, so they can run up walls to catch insects
Termite mound: thick earth walls and air passages that keep the nest fresh and cool
Pitcher plant: a slippery rim, so insects slide in and become their food
Honeybee comb: six-sided cells that hold the most honey for the least wax
Humpback whale: bumps on their flippers that help them turn tightly while hunting
Bird: twists the tips of their wings to balance and turn in the air

printables.title: 10 orange INVENTION cards to cut out
items: Velcro straps on shoes and bags
Wall paint that rain washes clean
The long nose of a quiet bullet train
A quieter arm on top of a bullet train, where it touches the electric wire
Tape and robot grippers that hold on with no glue
A building in Zimbabwe that stays cool with little air conditioning
A super-slippery coating that nothing sticks to
Light, strong panels inside aeroplane floors and doors
Bumpy-edged blades for wind turbines and fans
The Wright brothers' first aeroplane, which twisted its wingtips

printables.title: Design sheet
items: Pair found
The living thing's problem, and what the invention copied, in my own words
Points

rules: Cut out the 10 green nature cards and the 10 orange invention cards.
Shuffle each colour. Lay all 20 cards face down in rows, green on one side and orange on the other.
On your turn, turn over one green card and one orange card. Read both out loud.
If they are a pair, say what problem the living thing solves and what the invention copied, in your own words. Keep the pair and win 2 points. Then have another turn.
If they are not a pair, turn them back face down. Try to remember where they were.
A pair found without an explanation wins only 1 point.
When all the pairs are found, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone? Count your turns. Next time, try to finish in fewer turns.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Shuffle the green cards and lay them face down in two rows of 5. 3. Do the same with the orange cards, next to them.
flow.say: Every green card is a living thing with a problem in its own life, and the design that solves it. Every orange card is an invention that copied one of those designs. We will hunt for the pairs.
flow.kid: Lay the green cards face down. Lay the orange cards beside them. Each green card has one orange partner. Can you find them all?
flow.context: This is the first step of Nature's Idea Match, a memory game about inventions copied from plants and animals. Here you set up the cards.

flow.do: Play one practice pair face up. Show the burr card and the Velcro card side by side.
flow.say: Here is a pair to practise with. A burdock burr and Velcro. Why does the burr have hooks? And what did Velcro copy?
flow.kid: Practice pair: burr and Velcro. Why does the burr have hooks? What did Velcro copy?

ask.q: Why does the burr have hooks, and what did Velcro copy?
good: The hooks catch on fur, so animals carry its seeds away.
Velcro copied the hooks, and used loops in place of fur.

check.q: What design did Velcro copy from the burr?
options: Its tiny hooks, which catch in loops
Its green colour
Its sticky glue
check.why: A burr has no glue. It is covered in tiny stiff hooks that catch in fur and thread. Velcro copies that: one strip has hooks and the other has soft loops. Picking 'sticky glue' is a common guess, because things that stick usually have glue.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Turn one green card and one orange card. 2. If they match, the player explains the pair and keeps it. 3. If not, turn them back. 4. Write each found pair on the design sheet.
flow.say: When you find a pair, don't just say the names. Say what problem the living thing has, how its design solves it, and what the invention copied.
flow.kid: Turn one green card and one orange card. A pair? Explain it to win 2 points. If not, turn them back.
flow.parent: The pairs are: burr and Velcro (hooks). Lotus and self-cleaning paint (waxy bumps). Kingfisher and train nose (a front that widens slowly). Owl and the quiet train arm (soft, fringed edges). Gecko and gripper tape (tiny hairs). Termite mound and the Zimbabwe building (thick walls and air channels). Pitcher plant and slippery coating. Honeycomb and aeroplane panels (six-sided cells). Whale flipper and turbine blades (bumpy edges). Bird wings and the Wright brothers' plane (twisted wingtips). Accept any explanation in the child's own words.

flow.do: When a player finds the honeycomb pair, stop and look at the six-sided cells together.
flow.say: Bees build with six-sided cells. Bees make wax inside their own bodies, and it costs them a lot of food. Six-sided cells fit together with no gaps, and use little wax for the space they hold.
flow.kid: Look at the honeycomb card. Each cell has six sides. They fit together with no gaps. Engineers copy this to make strong, light panels.
flow.think: Wax costs bees a lot of food to make. Why would a shape that saves wax spread among bees over many generations?

flow.do: Count the points to find the winner. Then ask each player which design they would most like to use in their own invention.
flow.say: Which design would you most like to borrow for an invention of your own? What would you make with it?
flow.kid: Count your points. Playing alone? Write how many turns it took. Which design would you borrow for an invention?
flow.think: All these designs were found by people who looked very closely at living things. What living thing near you might be solving a problem that nobody has noticed yet?

games.title: Design Dice
games.context: This is an inventing game. You roll one die for a problem and one die for a living thing. Then you invent something that uses that living thing's design to solve the problem.

printables.title: Problem list (roll the first die)
items: 1 My water bottle gets warm in the sun
2 My school bag keeps sliding off the chair
3 My name label gets muddy in the rain
4 My paper boat sinks and gets soggy
5 My toy car is slow and noisy
6 Thatha's chappal slips on the wet bathroom floor

printables.title: Nature list (roll the second die)
items: 1 Burr: tiny hooks that catch
2 Lotus leaf: waxy bumps that make water roll off
3 Kingfisher: a pointed front that widens slowly
4 Gecko: millions of tiny bendy hairs
5 Termite mound: thick walls that slow heat
6 Tree frog: soft toe pads with grooves that let water out

printables.title: Inventor's score sheet
items: Problem
Living thing
My invention (draw it)
I named the design (1 point)
I said how to test it (1 point)
It could really be built (1 point)

rules: You need one die, or two dice, the two printed lists and the score sheet.
Roll the die once. Find that number on the Problem list.
Roll again. Find that number on the Nature list.
In 2 minutes, draw an invention that uses that living thing's design to solve that problem.
Explain it. Score 1 point for naming the design, 1 point for saying how you would test it, and 1 point if it could really be built.
If the pair seems impossible, you may roll the Nature die once more.
Play 5 rounds. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone? Try to beat your own best score.

flow.do: 1. Put the two printed lists and the score sheet on the table. 2. Have a die, a pencil and a timer ready.
flow.say: Inventors often start with a problem, then look at nature for a design. Today the dice will choose the problem and the living thing. You do the inventing.
flow.kid: Put out the two lists and your score sheet. Get a die and a pencil. The dice choose a problem and a living thing. You invent!
flow.context: This is the first step of Design Dice, an inventing game. You join a home problem with a design from nature.

flow.do: Play one round together as practice. Use problem 1, the warm water bottle, and nature 5, the termite mound.
flow.say: Practice round. The water bottle gets warm in the sun. The termite mound has thick walls that slow heat. What could we invent?
flow.kid: Practice: a warm water bottle, and a termite mound. How could thick walls help a water bottle? Draw your idea.

ask.q: How could you test if your bottle cover works?
good: Put two bottles in the sun, one with the cover. Feel which is cooler after an hour.
Put an ice cube in each and see which melts last.

check.q: A water bottle gets warm in the sun. Which idea copies the termite mound's design?
options: Wrap it in a thick jacket of cloth, so heat gets in slowly
Paint it shiny gold
Make it pointed like a beak
check.why: A termite mound's thick earth walls slow down the heat getting in. A thick cloth jacket does the same for a bottle. Wetting the cloth helps even more, like a clay water pot. Picking 'pointed like a beak' mixes up the designs. A pointed shape helps with moving through air or water, not with heat.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll both dice. 2. Each player draws an invention in 2 minutes. 3. They explain it. 4. The others score it with the three points on the sheet.
flow.say: Roll, draw for two minutes, then tell us about it. Remember the three points: name the design, say how to test it, and could it really be built?
flow.kid: Roll both dice. Draw your invention in 2 minutes. Then explain it, with the design and how to test it.
flow.parent: Some strong answers. A burr-hook strip on the bag strap and a loop strip on the chair, for problem 2. A label rubbed thickly with candle wax, for problem 3. A pointed nose for the toy car, for problem 5. Grooved soft rubber pads on the chappal, like a tree frog's toe pads, for problem 6. Silly but well-explained ideas deserve the first point too.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then choose the one invention everyone would most like to really build.
flow.say: Which invention should we really build and test? We can try it in the My Nature Invention project.
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which of your inventions would you most like to really build? Circle it.
flow.think: Some pairs seemed impossible at first, then turned into good ideas. Why does joining two very different things help us invent?
