items.p: Three of these copy how a living thing works. Which one only copies how a living thing looks?
opts: A teapot shaped like an elephant
Velcro, with hooks like a burr's
A paint that rain washes clean, like a lotus leaf
A train nose that widens slowly, like a kingfisher's beak
items.why: The teapot only looks like an elephant. It does not use anything an elephant's body does. The other three copy a working design: hooks, waxy bumps and a slowly widening front. A strong answer says what each of the other three copies.

items.p: In your own words, what is biomimicry? Give one example that is not Velcro.
items.a: Biomimicry is finding out how a living thing solves a problem in their life, and using the same idea to solve a human problem. For example, the lotus leaf's tiny waxy bumps make rain roll off, and self-cleaning paint copies them.
items.why: A strong answer has both parts: the living thing's own problem and how it solves it, and the human problem the copy solves.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Thrissur, sprinkles a little chalk dust on a chembu leaf. Then she drips water on the leaf and tilts it. What will the rolling drops do to the chalk dust?
opts: Pick it up and carry it off the leaf
Leave it exactly where it was
Turn it into mud that sticks to the leaf
items.why: The drops stay round and roll. As they roll, dust sticks to the water more than to the waxy bumps, so the drops carry it away. This is how a lotus leaf stays clean in a muddy pond. A strong answer says why the dust sticks to the drop and not to the leaf.

items.p: Velcro has tiny ____ on one strip and soft loops on the other.
items.why: The hooks on one strip catch in the loops on the other, just as a burr's hooks catch in an animal's fur.

items.p: In the splash experiment, the pancake made the most splash and the pointed beak made the least. A fourth shape is made from the same amount of dough: a short, fat cone. Where do you think its splash will be?
opts: Between the ball and the beak
items.why: The fat cone has a point, so it enters more gently than a ball. But it widens quickly, so it shoves more water at once than the long beak. A strong answer gives a reason from the shape: how quickly it gets wider.

items.p: Match each living thing to the invention that copied it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each invention copied one design: hooks, waxy bumps, a slowly widening front, tiny bendy hairs, and thick walls with air moving through them.

items.p: Sort each one by the problem it solves.
items: a burr
Holding on
a gecko's toes
Holding on
Velcro
Holding on
a lotus leaf
Staying clean and dry
self-cleaning paint
Staying clean and dry
a termite mound
Keeping cool
a clay water pot
Keeping cool
a thick-walled mud house
Keeping cool
items.a: see items
items.why: Living things and inventions that look nothing alike can solve the same problem. Sorting by problem, not by looks, is how inventors find ideas.

items.p: Some people think a gecko's feet are sticky, like glue. What could you check to show that this is wrong?
opts: Whether the gecko leaves glue marks on the glass
items.why: Glue would leave marks, and it would get dirty and stop working. Gecko feet leave no glue. They grip because hundreds of millions of tiny hair tips get so close to the wall that their atoms pull on the wall's atoms.

items.p: In the ice experiment, which cup house kept its ice the longest? Give your result, and explain it using the word 'walls'.
items.a: For example: the cup in thick newspaper kept its ice for 50 minutes, and the bare cup for only 20. Thick walls slow down the heat from the sun getting in, so the ice melts more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer gives the child's own numbers, and explains that walls slow heat getting in. They do not make cold.

items.p: To copy a living thing well, an invention must look like that living thing.
items.why: False. Good biomimicry copies how something works, not how it looks. Velcro looks nothing like a burdock plant, but it uses the same hooks. Many people guess 'true' at first.

items.p: The first bullet trains in Japan made a loud boom every time they came out of a tunnel. Why?
opts: They squeezed the air in front of them, and it burst out of the far end
items.why: A fast train pushes the air ahead of it, like a plunger in a pipe. The squeezed air rushes ahead and bursts out of the tunnel with a boom. Nothing broke. It was the air.

items.p: Two children in Bengaluru are arguing about who should get the credit for Velcro.

views.says: George de Mestral, the Swiss engineer. He spent about ten years making it work.
The burdock plant. The hooks were the plant's design long before any person thought of them.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it up. For de Mestral: the plant's hooks could not hold a shoe strap, and it took him years to find hooks and loops that work in cloth. For the plant: without the burr there would be no idea to copy. It then admits a fair point from the other side.
items.why: There is no single right answer. This is a question about what counts as inventing: having the design, or making it useful for people.

items.p: Put an inventor's steps in order.
items: Test it fairly
Find a problem
Improve it and test again
Find a living thing that solves the same problem
Build a rough first model
Draw a design
a: Find a living thing that solves the same problem
items.why: Inventors start with a problem, look for a living thing that solves it, plan, build a rough version, test it, then improve it. The last two steps can go round many times.

items.p: Draw a burr's hook catching a loop of wool. Label the hook and the loop.
items.a: A curved hook, like the letter J, caught through a round loop of wool, both labelled.
items.why: The hook catches in the loop, so they hold together. A strong drawing shows the hook going through the loop, not just touching it.
items.art: A blank box with a small loop of wool drawn in the corner.

items.p: In the leaf experiment, the drops on the smooth, shiny steel plate stayed as domes and often did not roll. The drops on the chembu leaf rolled away. What does this show?
opts: Smooth things always make water roll
Being smooth is not enough. The leaf's tiny bumps and wax make the difference
The steel plate was not tilted enough
items.why: Many people think smooth and shiny means slippery for water. The steel plate shows that is not so. The chembu leaf is bumpy and waxy, and that is what keeps the drops round so they roll.

items.p: Every kind of bird that dives into water has a long, pointed beak like a kingfisher's.
items.why: False. Brown pelicans plunge into the sea with a huge pouched beak. Cormorants and ducks dive from the surface with hooked or flat beaks. The kingfisher's long, slowly widening beak is one good answer to the splash problem, not the only one. A strong answer names another diving bird or says what else could help, such as folding the wings back.

items.p: Why does touching a lotus leaf with your fingers spoil the lotus effect in that spot?
items.why: The leaf's self-cleaning needs both the bumps and the wax. Rubbing wipes away the wax, so water can grip that spot and spread. 'Fingers are wet' is a fair thought, but even dry fingers rub off wax.

items.p: In the Lotus Spoon activity, the sooty spoon looked silver under water, but a clean spoon did not. Explain what the silver shine was, and how this is like a lotus leaf.
items.a: The soot is covered in tiny bumps. Water cannot push into the gaps between them, so a thin layer of air stays trapped there. Light bounces off the air and looks silver. A lotus leaf also keeps air between their bumps, so the water sits on top and rolls.
items.why: A strong answer names the trapped air and links it to the lotus leaf's bumps.

items.p: In the splash experiment, why must every dough shape have the same amount of dough and be dropped from the same height?
opts: Because 30 centimetres is a lucky height
So that only the shape changes, and we know the shape caused the difference
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. A heavier lump or a higher drop makes a bigger splash. Then you could not tell whether the shape or the weight made the difference.

items.p: One girl's splash results were pancake 22 spots, ball 9, beak 2. Her friend's results were pancake 15, ball 6, beak 1. The numbers are different. Do the two tests agree?
opts: No, because the numbers are different
No, so one of the tests must be wrong
Yes. Both show the same order: pancake most, beak least
items.why: The exact numbers depend on things like the bucket and the newspaper. What matters is the pattern, and both tests show the same pattern. A strong answer says that the order is what both tests found.

items.p: Eiji Nakatsu, a Japanese train engineer who loved watching birds, said the kingfisher and the bullet train have the same problem. What is the problem? Explain how the beak shape solves it.
items.a: Both push fast into something that cannot get out of the way quickly: the kingfisher into water, the train into the air inside a tunnel. A blunt front shoves it all at once, which makes a splash or a boom. A long front that widens slowly pushes it aside a little at a time.
items.why: A strong answer names both the water and the air, and explains 'a little at a time'.

items.p: Sharks, dolphins and penguins are not close relatives. But they all have a smooth, pointed shape. Explain why.
items.a: They all have to move fast through water. Over millions of years, the ones with shapes that slipped through water more easily caught more food and had more young. So all three ended up with a similar shape.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same problem, moving through water, led to the same answer in different animals. Scientists call this convergent evolution. Animals did not copy each other.

items.p: In the Gecko Toe Prints activity, you printed on wavy cardboard with a soft brush and with a flat eraser. Why did the brush print reach into the dips, but the eraser did not?
opts: The bristles bend into the dips, but a flat pad only touches the tops
items.why: A stiff, flat pad touches only the tops of the bumps. Bendy bristles spread into the dips. Gecko hairs do the same on a bumpy wall, so much more of the foot touches the wall.

items.p: A gecko lets go of a wall by pulling their whole foot straight off at once.
items.why: False. A gecko peels their toes up from the tips, like peeling tape from a corner. That breaks only a few hair grips at a time, so it takes almost no effort. Pulling straight off would mean breaking all the grips at once.

items.p: A termite mound needs air moving through it only to keep cool.
items.why: False. Millions of termites, and the fungus they grow inside, breathe out carbon dioxide. It must get out, and fresh air must get in, or they would suffocate. So the moving air does two jobs: it lets the mound breathe, and it helps keep it from getting too hot. A strong answer names both jobs.

items.p: A first, rough model of an invention, made to test an idea, is called a ____.
items.why: A prototype is a quick first try. Engineers expect it to have problems, because testing it shows how to make it better.

items.p: Around the year 1500, Leonardo da Vinci drew flying machines with flapping wings. None of them flew. In 1903, the Wright brothers' plane flew. What did the Wright brothers copy from birds?
opts: How birds twist their wingtips to balance
items.why: They copied a design, the twist of the wingtips, not the look of flapping. Flapping is what many early inventors tried, and it did not work for machines big enough to carry a person.

items.p: The Lotus Temple in Delhi is shaped like a lotus flower. Self-cleaning paint looks nothing like a lotus. Which one is biomimicry? Explain.
items.a: The self-cleaning paint is biomimicry. It copies the lotus leaf's tiny waxy bumps, so rain washes it clean. The temple only copies the look of the flower.
items.why: Biomimicry copies how something works. Copying only the look is art or decoration, which is lovely too, but different.

items.p: Scientists have made gecko tape with tiny hairs. It grips glass well, but after some uses it gets dusty and grips less. A real gecko's toes clean themselves as the gecko walks. What does this tell you about copying nature? Say what an inventor could try next.
items.a: It tells me a copy often takes only part of the design. The gecko's toes do two jobs, gripping and staying clean, and the tape copied only the gripping. An inventor could study how the gecko's toes shed dust as they walk, and try to copy that part too.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the living design solves more than one problem, and that a good copy has to find and copy each part that matters.

items.p: Two sisters in Chennai want to keep a bottle of water cool on a hot afternoon. Their cousin joins in.

views.says: Wrap it in thick newspaper. Thick walls slow the heat getting in, like a termite mound.
Wrap it in a wet cloth. As the water dries off, it cools the bottle, like a clay water pot.
Use both: newspaper next to the bottle, and a wet cloth outside.

items.ask: Which idea would you choose? Use your results from the ice experiment. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the child's own results. It may notice that a wet cloth cools best when the air is dry and breezy, and less in damp, still air like a Chennai afternoon, while newspaper works without any water. It admits a fair point from another side.
items.why: Each idea is a real way to keep things cool, and which works best depends on the weather. That is why testing beats arguing.

items.p: Draw a water drop sitting on a lotus leaf, as if you could see it from the side, very close up. Show the bumps, the wax and the air.
items.a: A round drop resting on the tips of bumps, a thin wax coat on each bump, and air in the gaps under the drop.
items.why: This shows why the drop stays round: it touches only the tips, and air fills the rest. A strong drawing shows the drop not sinking between the bumps.
items.art: A blank box with a wavy line across the bottom for the leaf.

items.p: Why is a big splash a problem for a kingfisher?
opts: The splash warns the fish, and slapping the water slows the bird down
The kingfisher cannot see in a splash
items.why: A kingfisher lives by catching small fish. A blunt head would slap the water, slow the bird down and send out ripples that warn the fish. A slowly widening beak solves the kingfisher's own problem, long before trains.

items.p: Deep down, why does water pull itself into a ball on a waxy leaf?
opts: Wax pushes water away with magnets
Water molecules pull on each other more strongly than the wax pulls on them
items.why: Water molecules tug on each other. Wax hardly pulls on water at all. So the water's own pull wins, and it gathers into a round drop. The pull between molecules is electric, but it is not magnetism.

items.p: In the cling film activity, the film held on to smooth glass and steel but fell off a towel and a rough wall. Use this to explain why a gecko needs millions of tiny, bendy hairs, not one flat pad.
items.a: Cling film grips only where it gets extremely close to a surface. On a rough wall, it touches only the tops of the bumps. A gecko's walls and trees are rough too. Millions of tiny bendy hairs can reach into the dips, so much more of the foot gets close enough to grip.
items.why: A strong answer links the result to 'getting very close', and explains why many tiny bendy tips beat one stiff pad on a bumpy surface.

items.p: Scientists have argued about how a gecko's toes grip a wall.

views.who: Kellar Autumn and his team, in the USA, 2000 and 2002
views.says: The grip comes from tiny electric pulls between atoms, called van der Waals forces. Gecko hairs grip even on dry surfaces that water cannot wet.

views.who: Gerrit Huber and others, in Germany, 2005
views.says: Gecko hairs grip harder in damp air. So a thin film of water from the air helps the grip too.

items.ask: Which side do you think the evidence supports more? Then say what the other side has right, and describe one test that could help settle it.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both findings can be true at once: the pull between atoms does most of the work, and damp air seems to add to it. A good test keeps the gecko and the surface the same and changes only how damp the air is.
items.why: Most scientists agree the pull between atoms does most of the work. How much water helps is still being studied.

items.p: The Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, was built in 1996 to copy how termite mounds were thought to stay cool, with air rising up a chimney. Later, scientists found that real mounds work differently. Was the building a failure? Explain what you think.
items.a: I think it was not a failure. It stays cool and uses much less power than other buildings, so the idea of thick walls and moving air worked. But it was not a true copy of a mound, because the old idea of how mounds work was wrong. It also uses fans at night.
items.why: A strong answer separates two questions: does the building work, and is it a true copy of a termite mound? A building can work well even if the science behind it was partly wrong.

items.p: Ananya, aged 8, says, 'A burr grows hooks after they touch an animal's fur.' What is wrong with her idea? Explain how burrs came to have hooks.
items.a: The hooks are already on the burr before it ever meets an animal. Over many generations, burdock plants with slightly better hooks got their seeds carried further, so more of those seeds grew. Their young had good hooks too. So the hooks got better and better.
items.why: A strong answer says the hooks come first, and explains change over many generations, not during one burr's life.

items.p: Which of these shows that nature's designs are not always perfect?
opts: Your eye has a blind spot, but an octopus eye does not
items.why: Evolution changes what is already there, a little at a time. Our eyes are wired in a way that leaves a blind spot. An octopus eye, which evolved separately, is wired the other way and has none. The other answers show designs working well.

items.p: In 2005, a car company made a car shaped like a boxfish, a small reef fish shaped like a box. Later, scientists studied real boxfish. What did they find the boxy shape mainly helps the fish to do?
opts: Swim very fast in a straight line
items.why: The car copied the shape to slip through the air. But the boxfish's shape mainly helps them turn and steer. The lesson: before copying a shape, find out what it is really for in the animal's own life.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one copy how a living thing works, or only how it looks?
items: a train nose that widens slowly, like a kingfisher's beak
Copies how it works
a dolphin-shaped swimming float
Copies only the look
a slippery coating copied from the inside of a pitcher plant
Copies how it works
a peacock-feather pattern printed on a sari
Copies only the look
gripper tape with tiny hairs, like a gecko's toes
Copies how it works
a butterfly-shaped hair clip
Copies only the look
items.a: see items
items.why: Copying the working part solves a problem. Copying the look decorates. A strong answer can say what working part each 'how it works' item copies.

items.p: In the fastener challenge, 4 paper clip hooks held a towel with 6 coins. About how many coins would 12 hooks hold, if each hook holds the same?
items.why: 12 hooks is 3 lots of 4 hooks. 3 times 6 is 18. Picking 12 means matching the coins to the number of hooks, instead of using the pattern. Real results may wobble a little, because not every hook catches equally well.

items.p: Is a bullet train natural or made by people? Give a reason for your answer, and one reason someone might disagree.
items.a: I think it is made by people, because people designed and built it. But someone might say it is natural too, because its nose copies a kingfisher's beak, and people are part of nature.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer gives a reason, and states another view fairly.

items.p: Invent something that copies a living thing you saw this week. Draw it, label the design you copied, and write how you would test it fairly.
items.a: Any invention with a labelled design from a real living thing, and a fair test where only one thing changes.
items.why: Inventing means joining a problem, a design from nature and a fair test. Real engineers do exactly this.
items.art: A blank inventor's page with a box for the drawing and lines for 'design copied' and 'my test'.

items.p: The arm on top of a bullet train, which touches the electric wire, was very noisy. Engineers gave it jagged edges, copied from an owl's feathers. Why might these edges make it quieter?
opts: The jagged edges keep the wire cool
Owl feathers are lighter than metal
Soft, fringed edges break the moving air into small swirls that make less noise
The edges stop rain getting in
items.why: Owls fly with almost no sound, because the edges of their feathers are soft and fringed. A smooth, hard edge makes big swirls of air that roar. Fringed edges break the air up into tiny swirls, which are much quieter.

items.p: Nature's designs have been tested for millions of years, so copying them always gives the best answer.
items.why: False. A design solves the living thing's own problem, in their own life, and it is built from what their ancestors already had. The boxfish car and our eye's blind spot show that copying needs care. A strong answer gives one example.

items.p: Put these in order, to show why a blunt-nosed train made a boom coming out of a tunnel.
items: The squeezed air bursts out of the far end with a loud boom
A blunt-nosed train rushes into the tunnel
The air inside cannot get out of the way fast enough
A wave of squeezed air races ahead of the train along the tunnel
a: A blunt-nosed train rushes into the tunnel
The air inside cannot get out of the way fast enough
A wave of squeezed air races ahead of the train along the tunnel
The squeezed air bursts out of the far end with a loud boom
items.why: Each step causes the next. A long nose that widens slowly squeezes the air a little at a time, so the wave is weaker and the boom is much quieter.

items.p: When animals that are not closely related end up with the same shape, because they face the same problem, it is called ____ evolution.
items.why: 'Converge' means to come together. Sharks, dolphins and penguins came to the same streamlined shape from different starting points.

experiments.title: The Leaf That Water Can't Wet
experiments.context: A lotus leaf must keep itself clean, because dirt would block the sunlight it needs. In this experiment you drip water on a lotus-like leaf and on other surfaces, tilt them, and see which ones the water rolls off. Then you see if rolling drops can clean away dust.
experiments.question: Which surface makes water roll off in balls? Can rolling drops clean a surface?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the water make round balls, flat puddles or wet patches on the leaf, the steel plate and the paper? Which will stay cleanest when dusty? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the surface. Use the same size of drop, from the same spoon or dropper. Tilt every surface to the same height, on the same book. Put 5 drops on each surface, because one drop can be a fluke.
results_table: Drop shape: ball, dome or flat
How many of 5 drops rolled off at the tilt
Did the rolling drops pick up the dust?

materials.item: one water-repelling leaf: a chembu (colocasia, also called arbi) leaf from the vegetable market, a lotus leaf, a nasturtium leaf, or the outer leaf of a cabbage
one ordinary leaf, like a tulsi, money plant or mango leaf
a steel plate and a sheet of paper
a dropper, or a spoon, or a straw (dip it in water and cover the top with your finger)
a small bowl of water
a pinch of chalk dust (rub chalk on rough paper) or a pinch of haldi powder
a thick book, about 3 cm thick, for tilting
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: Haldi stains clothes and fingers yellow. Use chalk dust if you prefer. Wash your hands after touching leaves from outside.

schedule.what: Drip water on four surfaces, tilt them, and do the dust test. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what a drop looked like from the side on each surface: a ball, a dome or a flat puddle.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four surfaces flat on a tray or the floor. They are the water-repelling leaf, the ordinary leaf, the steel plate and the paper. 2. Hold each leaf only by its stalk or its edge. 3. Ask your child to guess what water will do on each.
flow.say: Don't touch the top of the leaves with your fingers. Your fingers can rub off the leaf's coat of wax. What do you think water will do on each one?
flow.kid: Lay out the two leaves, the steel plate and the paper. Hold leaves by the stalk only. Guess: on which one will water roll?
flow.parent: Touching or rubbing the top of a lotus or chembu leaf wipes off its wax. Then that spot gets wet like any leaf. Old, dusty or bruised leaves work less well. Pick a fresh one.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Leaf That Water Can't Wet. You set out a lotus-like leaf and three other surfaces to test with water.

flow.do: 1. Put 5 drops of water on each surface, spaced apart. 2. Crouch down so your eyes are level with the surface. 3. Look at the drops from the side.
flow.say: Get your eyes down low and look at the drops from the side. Are they round like balls, like little domes, or flat?
flow.kid: Put 5 drops on each one. Get your eyes down low. Look from the side. Balls, domes, or flat puddles?

ask.q: What do the drops on the chembu leaf look like?
good: Little silver balls.
Like marbles.
They are round and shiny.

flow.parent: On a good chembu or lotus leaf, the drops look like silver balls or beads of mercury. On steel, they are low domes. On paper, they soak in within a minute. On an ordinary leaf, they spread into flat puddles. On a cabbage leaf, the drops bead up well but are a little flatter than on chembu.

flow.do: 1. Put one end of each surface on the book, so it is tilted. 2. Count how many of the 5 drops roll off. 3. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: Let's tilt each one onto the book. Count: how many of the five drops roll away?
flow.kid: Lift one end of each onto the book. Count how many drops roll off. Write it down.

check.q: On which surface did the drops roll off most easily?
options: The chembu or lotus leaf
The paper
The ordinary leaf
check.why: The chembu or lotus leaf is covered in tiny waxy bumps. A drop sits only on the bump tips, with air under it, so it stays round and rolls at a small tilt. Paper pulls the water in, so it soaks. Picking the ordinary leaf usually means thinking all leaves are the same. Most leaves have no bumps like this, so water spreads on them.

flow.do: 1. Lay the water-repelling leaf and the paper flat again. 2. Sprinkle a thin pinch of chalk dust or haldi on each. 3. Tilt them on the book. 4. Drip drops at the top end, one at a time, and watch them roll down.
flow.say: Now our leaf is dusty, like a lotus in a dirty pond. Watch the drop as it rolls. What happens to the dust?
flow.kid: Sprinkle a little dust on the leaf and the paper. Tilt them. Drip drops at the top. Watch what happens to the dust!

ask.q: What did the rolling drop do on the leaf?
good: It picked up the dust.
It left a clean path behind it.
The dust went into the drop.

flow.think: Did you need to wipe or scrub the leaf? How did it clean itself?
flow.parent: On the leaf, each rolling drop gathers the dust and leaves a clean stripe behind. Look with the magnifying glass if you have one. On the paper, the water soaks in and the dust becomes a wet smudge. If drops stick on your leaf, try a fresher leaf, or a spot you have not touched. This is how a lotus keeps clean. Every shower of rain washes their leaves, so they stay clear for sunlight.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the chembu leaf keeps itself clean. What I saw: all 5 drops rolled off it, and they picked up the chalk dust. On paper, no drops rolled and the dust made a smudge. Why: the leaf has tiny waxy bumps, so water makes balls that roll and carry dirt away.

experiments.title: Splash Like a Kingfisher
experiments.context: In this unit's story, a kingfisher dives with hardly a splash, and a bullet train copies their beak. In this experiment you drop dough shapes into a bucket of water and count the splash drops.
experiments.question: Which shape goes into water with the smallest splash: a flat pancake, a round ball, or a long pointed beak?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the three shapes in order, from the one you think will splash most to the one you think will splash least. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the shape. Use the same amount of dough for each shape. Drop each one from the same height, 30 cm above the water, measured with a ruler. Keep the water at the same level, 3 cm below the rim. Use a dry sheet of newspaper each time. Drop each shape 3 times.

materials.item: a bucket, filled with water to about 3 cm below the rim
atta dough, about one fist-sized lump, or play clay
4 or 5 sheets of old newspaper, to lay around the bucket
a ruler
a kitchen scale, if you have one

experiments.safety: Do this outside, in the bathroom, or on a floor you can mop. Wipe up spilled water straight away, so nobody slips. Throw the used dough away. Don't eat it.

schedule.what: Make three dough shapes. Drop each into the bucket 3 times and count the splash spots on the newspaper.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each shape's middle value.

flow.do: 1. Divide the dough into three equal balls, each about the size of a lemon. If you have a kitchen scale, make each one 40 grams. 2. Leave one as a ball. 3. Press one flat into a pancake, about as wide as your palm. 4. Roll one into a long cone, thin and pointed at one end, getting wider slowly, like a kingfisher's beak.
flow.say: All three shapes have exactly the same amount of dough. Only the shape is different. So if one splashes less, it must be because of its shape.
flow.kid: Make three equal balls of dough. Keep one as a ball. Press one flat like a pancake. Roll one into a long pointed beak.
flow.context: This is the first step of Splash Like a Kingfisher. You make three dough shapes with the same amount of dough.

flow.do: 1. Put the bucket in the middle of the newspaper sheets, so the paper covers the floor all around it. 2. Check the water is 3 cm below the rim. 3. Hold the ruler upright from the water, to find 30 cm above it.
flow.say: Any splash that jumps out of the bucket will land on the newspaper and leave a wet spot. We'll count the spots.
flow.kid: Put newspaper all around the bucket. Splashes will make wet spots on it. Find 30 cm above the water with your ruler.

flow.do: 1. Hold the pancake flat, 30 cm above the water, and let go. 2. Count the wet spots on the newspaper. 3. Write the number down. 4. Lift out the dough and change to dry newspaper. 5. Do the same with the ball, then the beak. Hold the beak by its wide end, point down. 6. Do 3 tries for each shape.
flow.say: Let go, don't throw. Listen as it hits the water. Then let's count the spots.
flow.kid: Let go from 30 cm, don't throw. Listen! Count the wet spots on fresh newspaper. Do each shape 3 times.
flow.parent: The flat pancake usually slaps the water loudly and throws out many drops, often 15 or more. The ball splashes less. The beak, if it falls point first, goes in with a quiet 'ploop' and few or no spots. If the beak tumbles and lands on its side, that try doesn't count. If it keeps tumbling, do all three shapes again from 20 cm, to keep the test fair. If no shape throws spots out of the bucket, fill the bucket a little fuller.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Find the middle value for each shape. 2. Draw a bar chart, one bar for each shape.
flow.say: Each shape gets one bar. The taller the bar, the bigger the splash.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each shape. A taller bar means a bigger splash. Which shape is most like a kingfisher?

check.q: Why does the pointed beak shape splash least?
options: It pushes the water aside a little at a time, from its tip backwards
It is lighter than the other shapes
It falls more slowly
check.why: All three shapes had the same amount of dough, so they weighed the same. The flat pancake hits a lot of water at once, so the water is shoved hard and sprays out. The beak's thin tip goes in first, and it gets wider slowly. So it pushes water aside gently, a little at a time. Picking 'lighter' forgets that this was a fair test with the same amount of dough in each shape.

flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a long pointed shape goes into water with the smallest splash. What I saw: the pancake made 22 spots, the ball 9 and the beak only 2. Why: the beak pushes the water aside slowly, from its tip, like a kingfisher's beak. The same idea made the bullet train quieter in tunnels.

experiments.title: Keep the Ice: Walls Like a Termite Mound
experiments.context: Termite mounds stay cool inside on hot days, partly because their thick earth walls slow the heat down. In this experiment you build little houses with different walls, put an ice cube in each, and see which keeps its ice longest in the sun.
experiments.question: Which walls keep a little house coolest in the sun: thin walls, thick dry walls, or thick wet walls?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In which cup will the ice cube last longest? In which will it melt first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the walls. Use the same kind of cup, and ice cubes of the same size from the same tray. Put all the cups out at the same time, in the same sunny spot. Cover every cup with the same card lid. Check them all at the same times.
results_table: Time when the ice was all gone (minutes)

materials.item: 3 or 4 paper cups or small steel tumblers, all the same
3 or 4 ice cubes of the same size, from the same tray
old newspaper, and a rubber band or string
an old cotton cloth or hanky, and some water
4 small squares of card, for lids
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: Don't stay out in strong midday sun while you wait. Put the cups in the sun and wait in the shade. Drink some water.

schedule.what: Build the cup houses, put the ice in, and check every 10 minutes until the ice is gone.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart of how many minutes each ice cube lasted.

flow.do: 1. House A: leave one cup bare. These are thin walls. 2. House B: wrap one cup round and round in 3 sheets of newspaper, to make a thick wall. Hold it with a rubber band. These are thick dry walls, like a mound's earth. 3. House C: wrap one cup in a cotton cloth folded 4 times, soaked in water and squeezed so it does not drip. These are thick wet walls. 4. House D is your own design, if you want one.
flow.say: Termite mounds have thick earth walls. Let's see if thick walls really keep the heat out. Each cup is a little house.
flow.kid: Make three cup houses. Leave one bare. Wrap one in thick newspaper, and one in a wet cloth. Want to invent a fourth?
flow.parent: Here are good ideas for a fourth house. Cover a cup in white paper, or in black paper. Or stand a cup in a bowl of damp soil. Use the same size of cup.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep the Ice. You build little cup houses with different walls, to see which keeps an ice cube longest.

flow.do: 1. Put one ice cube in each cup. 2. Cover each cup with a card lid. 3. Put all the cups side by side in the sun. 4. Start the timer.
flow.say: All the cups go in the same sunny spot at the same time. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Put one ice cube in each cup. Put on the lids. Put all the cups in the sun together. Start the timer!

flow.do: 1. Every 10 minutes, lift each lid and look at the ice. 2. Write 'big', 'small' or 'gone' in the table. 3. Write the time when each cube has fully melted.
flow.say: Let's peek every ten minutes. Lift the lid, look, and put it back quickly.
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, peek under each lid. Is the ice big, small or gone? Write it down.
flow.wait: Check every 10 minutes until the ice in House A has melted. Leave the others until they melt too, if you can.
flow.parent: In strong Indian sun, the ice in a bare paper cup with a lid usually melts in about 20 to 40 minutes. While you wait, you can play Nature's Idea Match in the shade. The newspaper and wet-cloth houses often last twice as long or more. On a hot, dry day, the wet cloth often wins, because drying water takes heat away, like a clay water pot. On a humid monsoon day, the wet cloth works less well. On a cloudy day, do the test indoors by a window. It will take about an hour, so check every 15 minutes.

flow.do: Compare the times. Then talk about how the termite mound and old Indian houses keep cool.
flow.say: Thick walls slow down the heat getting in. Termites need this, because their fungus garden grows well only when the nest stays warm but not hot. Old mud houses use thick walls too.
flow.kid: Which house kept its ice longest? Thick walls slow down heat. Termite mounds and mud houses have thick walls too!

check.q: Why did the ice last longer in the thick-walled cup?
options: The thick wall slowed down the heat getting in
The thick wall made cold
The thick wall kept the light out, and light is what melts ice
check.why: Walls do not make cold. Heat from the sun is always trying to get into the cup. A thick wall slows the heat down, so the ice melts more slowly. A wet wall also loses heat as its water dries off, which cools it. Picking 'made cold' is a common idea. But cold is really just less heat.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: thick walls keep a house cooler, and wet thick walls are even better. What I saw: the bare cup's ice was gone at 25 minutes. The newspaper cup's lasted 50, and the wet cloth cup's 60. Why: thick walls slow the heat down, and drying water carries heat away, like on a clay water pot.

activities.title: The Hitchhiker Sock Walk
activities.context: If you have a park, a field or an empty plot nearby, try this walk. Some plants send their seeds travelling on animals, using hooks and spikes. You wear a fluffy sock over one shoe and a smooth one over the other, to see which carries more seeds home.

materials.item: one old fluffy woollen sock, or a strip of old towel, big enough to pull over a shoe
one smooth sock, like a thin nylon sock, or a plastic bag tied over the other shoe
closed shoes and long trousers
a paper bag or envelope for the seeds, and a magnifying glass if you have one

activities.safety: Go only with a grown-up, in daylight. Walk on short weeds at the edge of a park, a field or an empty plot, not in long grass where snakes may hide. Stamp your feet as you walk. Wash your hands afterwards and never put seeds in your mouth.

schedule.what: Walk through weeds with a fluffy sock and a smooth sock over your shoes. Count and sort the seeds that ride home.

activities.record: Write how many seeds stuck to the fluffy sock and how many to the smooth one. Draw the three strangest seeds, as big as you can.

flow.do: 1. Pull the fluffy sock over one shoe, and the smooth sock or plastic bag over the other. 2. Ask your child to guess which will collect more seeds.
flow.say: Some plants send their seeds travelling on animals. Seeds carried far away get new ground to grow in. Today, you are the animal. Which sock do you think will carry more seeds home, and why?
flow.kid: Pull a fluffy sock over one shoe. Put a smooth sock over the other. Which will collect more seeds? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hitchhiker Sock Walk. You get ready to collect seeds that stick to clothes, like burrs.

flow.do: Walk slowly through a patch of dry, short weeds for about 5 minutes. Brush both feet through the same plants.
flow.say: Walk slowly and brush both feet through the same weeds. That keeps it fair.
flow.kid: Walk slowly through the weeds for 5 minutes. Brush both feet through the same plants.
flow.parent: The best time is after the monsoon, from about September to February, when weeds are full of dry seeds. Good plants to brush past include chirchita (also called apamarg), cocklebur and sticky grasses. In summer there may be fewer seeds. If you find none, look along the edge of a playground or a railway fence, or try again next month.

flow.do: 1. Back home, take the socks off carefully. 2. Pick off the seeds and count them for each sock. 3. Look at a few with a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Let's count. Then look closely. How is each seed holding on? Hooks, spikes, or something sticky?
flow.kid: Count the seeds on each sock. Write the numbers down. Look closely. How does each seed hold on?

ask.q: Why did more seeds stick to the fluffy sock?
good: The hooks caught in the fluffy loops.
Smooth socks have nothing for hooks to grab.

check.q: Most seeds rode home on the fluffy sock. Why?
options: Their tiny hooks caught in its loops of wool
The fluffy sock was sticky
The seeds liked the colour
check.why: Hitchhiker seeds have tiny hooks or spikes. Hooks need something to catch on, like loops of wool or fur. A smooth sock has no loops, so the seeds slip off. This is exactly how Velcro works: hooks on one side, loops on the other. Picking 'sticky' is a common guess, but there is no glue on the sock or the seeds.

flow.do: Look at a Velcro strap next to the seeds, with the magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: George de Mestral looked at burrs like these under a microscope in 1941. He saw hooks caught in loops. So he made Velcro, with hooks on one strip and loops on the other. Can you see them?
flow.kid: Look at a Velcro strap. Can you see tiny hooks on one side, and loops on the other? A burr gave someone this idea!
flow.think: These seeds rode home with you, just as they ride on animals. Where could we put them, so they get a chance to grow?

activities.title: Zoom In Like an Inventor
activities.context: This activity is about looking very closely, the way George de Mestral looked at a burr. You use a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in, to look at Velcro, leaves, feathers and seeds.

materials.item: a magnifying glass, or a phone camera that can zoom in
a Velcro strap, a burr or sticky seed, a leaf, a feather, and a piece of fluffy wool
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass. It can hurt your eyes badly.

schedule.what: Look at five things very closely. Draw them as big as your page.

activities.record: Draw each thing as big as you can, the way it looks zoomed in. Label one feature you can see on each, and say what it might be for.

flow.do: 1. Put the five things on a table near a window, in good light. 2. Look at the hook side and the loop side of the Velcro. 3. Then look at the burr or sticky seed.
flow.say: Inventors notice tiny things. Look at both sides of the Velcro. Now look at the seed. What is the same?
flow.kid: Look at the Velcro up close. Then look at the seed. Can you see hooks on both?
flow.context: This is the first step of Zoom In Like an Inventor. You look at Velcro and a seed very closely, to find their hooks.

flow.do: 1. Look at the feather. Gently pull two parts of it apart, then stroke them back together. 2. Look at the leaf. 3. Look at the wool.
flow.say: Pull the feather apart a little, then stroke it from the bottom to the tip. Watch it zip back together. Feathers have tiny hooks too.
flow.kid: Pull a feather apart gently. Now stroke it back together. It zips up! Feathers have tiny hooks inside.
flow.parent: Each feather has rows of branches called barbs. The barbs carry even smaller branches called barbules, and these have tiny hooks that zip them together, like Velcro. A bird needs their feathers zipped into smooth sheets to fly. They re-zip them by running them through their beak. A strong magnifying glass shows the rows. You may not see the hooks themselves, which is fine.

flow.do: Help your child draw their two favourite things, very big, and label one feature on each.
flow.say: Draw it as if it were the size of a house. What feature can you see? What do you think it is for?
flow.kid: Draw your two favourite things, really big. Label one feature on each, like hooks, hairs or bumps.
flow.think: If a gecko walks on the outside of your window at night, look at their toes from inside. What do you see?

activities.title: Gecko Toe Prints
activities.context: A gecko's toes have millions of tiny bendy hairs that reach into the dips of a bumpy wall. In this activity you print with paint to see why bendy tips touch more of a bumpy surface than a flat pad does.

materials.item: a piece of corrugated cardboard from a box, with the top paper layer peeled off to show the wavy ridges
a flat eraser or a flat piece of sponge
a soft paintbrush with long bristles, or an old soft toothbrush
watercolour paint or poster paint, and a saucer

activities.safety: Cover the table with newspaper. Wash the brush afterwards.

schedule.what: Print with a flat pad and with bristles on wavy cardboard, and compare.

activities.record: Keep the two prints. Write which one touched more of the wavy surface.

flow.do: 1. Peel the top paper off one corner of the cardboard, so the wavy layer shows. 2. Dab paint on the flat eraser or sponge. 3. Press it straight down onto the wavy part, then lift it.
flow.say: This flat pad is like a hard, flat foot. Look at the print it leaves. Where did the paint go?
flow.kid: Paint the flat eraser. Press it straight down on the wavy cardboard. Lift it. Where is the paint?
flow.context: This is the first step of Gecko Toe Prints. You press a flat painted pad onto bumpy cardboard to see how much it touches.

flow.do: 1. Load the brush with paint. 2. Press it straight down, bristles first, onto a fresh wavy part, so the bristles splay out. 3. Lift it and compare the two prints.
flow.say: Now the brush. Its bristles are like a gecko's tiny hairs. Press it straight down, like a stamp. Compare the two prints.
flow.kid: Load the brush with paint. Press it straight down, like a stamp. Lift it. Which print has more paint in the dips?

ask.q: What is different about the two prints?
good: The flat pad only painted the tops of the waves.
The brush got paint down into the dips too.

flow.parent: The flat pad prints only stripes along the tops of the ridges. The bristles bend and reach into the dips, so far more of the surface gets paint. If the brush is stiff, press more gently, or use a softer brush.

flow.do: Talk about how this is like a gecko's foot.
flow.say: A real wall looks flat, but zoomed in it is bumpy, like this cardboard. A gecko's tiny hairs bend into all the bumps. The closer they get, the more the atoms of the hairs and the wall pull on each other.
flow.kid: Walls are bumpy when you zoom in. Gecko hairs bend into the bumps, like your brush. More touching means more grip.

check.q: Why do a gecko's tiny bendy hairs help them grip a bumpy wall?
options: They reach into the dips, so much more of the foot touches the wall
They are covered in glue
They suck onto the wall like a suction cup
check.why: Atoms only pull on each other when they get extremely close. A flat, stiff foot touches only the tops of the bumps. Millions of tiny bendy hairs reach into the dips, so far more of them touch. All those tiny pulls add up to a strong grip. Gecko feet have no glue and are not suction cups.

activities.title: How Close Is Close? (cling film)
activities.context: Things grip without glue only when they get extremely close, which is the gecko's secret. In this activity you press cling film onto different surfaces to see which ones it holds on to.

materials.item: a roll of cling film, the thin plastic wrap used for food
a steel plate, a mirror or a window, a plastic box, a wooden table, a towel, and a cement or brick wall

activities.safety: Never put cling film near your mouth or nose, or over anyone's face. Throw used pieces in the bin.

schedule.what: Press cling film onto six surfaces. See which ones it clings to.

activities.record: Make two lists: surfaces the film clung to, and surfaces it fell off.

flow.do: 1. Tear off six pieces of cling film, each about the size of your palm. 2. Press one flat onto each surface, smoothing it with dry fingers. 3. Turn the plate or box upside down, or wait 10 seconds on the wall, and see if it stays.
flow.say: Cling film has no glue. Let's see which surfaces it will hold on to by itself.
flow.kid: Press cling film onto each surface. Smooth it flat. Turn it upside down. Does the film stay on?
flow.context: This is the first step of How Close Is Close? You test which surfaces cling film holds on to without any glue.

flow.do: Compare the lists. Talk about why smooth, hard surfaces worked best.
flow.say: On smooth steel and glass, the film can get extremely close. Then the atoms of the film and the plate pull on each other. On a towel or a rough wall, the film touches only a few tips, so it falls off. Static electricity helps the film cling too.
flow.kid: The film clings to smooth glass and steel. It falls off towels and rough walls. Why? It can't get close enough to them.
flow.parent: Cling film holds on partly by getting very close to smooth surfaces, where atoms attract, and partly by static electricity. A gecko's feet get close even to rough surfaces, using millions of bendy hair tips. Expect the film to cling to the steel, the mirror and usually the plastic box. It falls off the towel and the wall.

check.q: Cling film stuck to the steel plate but fell off the towel. Why?
options: On smooth steel it could get very close, so the atoms pulled on each other
The towel was too heavy
Steel is magnetic, and cling film is a magnet
check.why: Atoms pull on each other only when they are extremely close. Smooth steel lets the film lie flat against almost all of it. A fluffy towel only lets it touch a few tips. Picking 'magnetic' is a sensible guess, but cling film is plastic and is not a magnet. It clings to glass too, which is not magnetic.

activities.title: Make a Lotus Spoon
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up coats the back of a steel spoon with candle soot, which makes tiny bumps like a lotus leaf. Then you see water roll off it in silver balls.

materials.item: an old steel spoon you don't need for eating
a candle on a steel plate, and a matchbox
a clothes peg or kitchen tongs, to hold the spoon
a glass of water and a dropper or a straw

activities.safety: Only a grown-up lights the candle and holds the spoon in the flame. Tie back long hair. Keep a glass of water nearby. The spoon gets hot: let it cool for 2 minutes before anyone touches it. Soot is dirty, so don't use the spoon for food afterwards.

schedule.what: A grown-up coats a spoon with soot. Drip water on it and dip it in water.

activities.record: Draw a drop on the clean side of the spoon and a drop on the sooty side.

flow.do: 1. Light the candle. 2. Hold the spoon with the peg or tongs. 3. Hold the back of the spoon in the yellow tip of the flame. Move it slowly for about 30 seconds, until the back is evenly black. 4. Blow out the candle. Let the spoon cool for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Watch the black soot build up on the spoon. Soot is made of tiny bits of carbon, smaller than dust. They pile up in tiny bumps, a bit like the lotus leaf's bumps.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to do this part. Watch from a safe distance. The spoon turns black with soot. Wait for it to cool.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Lotus Spoon. A grown-up covers the back of a spoon with candle soot.

flow.do: 1. Hold the cool spoon by its handle. Don't touch the soot. 2. Drip a few drops on the clean front of the spoon. 3. Drip a few drops on the sooty back. 4. Tilt it a little.
flow.say: Look at the drops on the clean side and on the sooty side. Tilt it. What happens?
flow.kid: Drip water on the clean side. Now on the sooty side. Tilt the spoon. Which drops roll away like marbles?

ask.q: What do the drops do on the soot?
good: They make balls and roll off.
They bounce and roll like on a lotus leaf.

flow.parent: On the sooty side, drops make almost perfect silver balls and roll off at the smallest tilt. On the clean steel, they sit as flat domes. If the drops stick to the soot, the layer may be too thin. A grown-up can add another 20 seconds in the flame. If you touch the soot, that spot will stop working.

flow.do: Slowly dip the sooty back of the spoon into the glass of water, and look at it from the side.
flow.say: Dip it slowly into the water. Look closely. Does the black spoon still look black?
flow.kid: Dip the sooty spoon slowly into the water. Look from the side. What colour does it look now?
flow.think: The spoon looks silver under water. That silver is a thin skin of air, trapped between the bumps. Could the air be what keeps it dry?

check.q: Under water, the sooty spoon looks shiny silver. What is the silver?
options: A thin layer of air trapped in the tiny bumps
The steel showing through
The soot turning into metal
check.why: The soot is covered in tiny bumps. Water cannot push into the spaces between them, so a thin skin of air stays trapped there. Light bounces off that air layer, so it looks silver like a mirror. A lotus leaf under water shines silver for the same reason. Picking 'the steel showing through' is a fair guess, but the soot is still there when you lift it out.

activities.title: Beak Hand, Flat Hand
activities.context: This is a quick activity to feel drag, the push of water against a moving thing. You move your hand through water flat, and then shaped like a kingfisher's beak.

materials.item: a bucket or a big basin of water

activities.safety: Do this outside or in the bathroom. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Push your hand through water flat, then like a beak. Feel the difference.

activities.record: Draw your flat hand and your beak hand. Draw arrows showing how hard the water pushed back on each.

flow.do: 1. Put your hand in the water with the palm facing forward, like a wall. 2. Sweep it quickly from one side of the bucket to the other.
flow.say: Sweep your flat hand through the water. Feel how hard the water pushes back. Look at the splash.
flow.kid: Put your hand in the water, palm forward like a wall. Sweep it fast. Feel the water push back?
flow.context: This is the first step of Beak Hand, Flat Hand. You feel how hard water pushes back on a flat hand.

flow.do: 1. Now press your fingers tightly together into a point, like a kingfisher's beak. 2. Turn your hand so the fingertips point the way you will move. 3. Sweep it through the water at the same speed.
flow.say: Now make a beak with your fingers, and lead with the tip. Sweep at the same speed. What's different?
flow.kid: Make a beak with your fingers. Lead with the tip. Sweep at the same speed. Is it easier?

ask.q: Which hand was easier to move through the water?
good: The beak hand.
The pointed one slid through, the flat one was pushed back.

flow.do: Talk about the kingfisher and the bullet train.
flow.say: The flat hand shoves a lot of water at once. The beak hand pushes the water aside a little at a time. Kingfishers dive like your beak hand. A Japanese bullet train copied this shape for its nose.
flow.kid: The flat hand shoves lots of water at once. The beak hand parts it slowly. Kingfishers dive like a beak hand!

check.q: Why was the beak hand easier to move through the water?
options: It pushed the water aside a little at a time
Your fingers were stronger when they were together
There was less water in the bucket
check.why: The push of water on a moving thing is called drag. A flat hand meets a lot of water all at once, so drag is big. A pointed hand meets the water with its tip first and widens slowly, so it parts the water gently and the drag is smaller. Picking 'stronger fingers' misses that the same hand, at the same speed, changed only its shape.

projects.title: My Nature Invention
projects.context: In this 3-day project you become a biomimicry inventor. You pick a real problem at home, find a living thing that solves a problem like it, then design, build, test and improve your own invention.

materials.item: paper, pencils and colours for designing
building things from home: cardboard, paper cups, string, sticky tape, paperclips, old cloth, an old sock, rubber bands, candle wax, foil, newspaper
things for testing: a ruler, coins, a dropper or spoon, ice cubes, a clock
scissors with round tips

projects.safety: A grown-up does any cutting with a sharp knife and anything with a flame. Use round-tipped scissors. Test inventions somewhere safe, away from stairs.

schedule.what: Choose a problem. Find a living thing that solves a problem like it. Draw a labelled plan.
Build a prototype. Test it fairly against the plain version. Write the results.
Improve the design and test again. Make an invention poster and show it to the family.

projects.record: Keep an inventor's notebook page. Write the problem, the living thing and its design, a labelled drawing, the test results before and after improving, and what you changed.

flow.do: Walk around the home together and list three small problems. Maybe a bag slides off a chair, or a bottle gets warm. Maybe a label gets dirty, or a bathroom mat slips.
flow.say: Inventors start with a problem, not with a gadget. Let's find three small problems in our home that annoy someone.
flow.kid: Walk around your home. Find three small problems. Look for things that slip, get hot or get dirty.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Nature Invention, a 3-day project. You start by finding a real problem at home to solve.

flow.do: Choose one problem. Then ask: which living thing has a problem like this, and how does it solve it? Use the cards from Nature's Idea Match if you made them.
flow.say: Pick one problem. Now ask the inventor's question. Which living thing has a problem like this in its own life? How does it solve it?
flow.kid: Pick one problem. Which plant or animal has this problem too? How do they solve it?
flow.parent: Helpful pairs. Things slipping: burr hooks, gecko hairs, tree frog toe pads. Getting dirty or wet: the lotus leaf. Getting hot: the termite mound and the clay water pot. Moving through air or water: the kingfisher. Let the child choose, even if their idea seems odd. The test will show what works.

ask.q: What exactly will you copy, and what does it do for the living thing?
good: The burr's hooks, which catch in fur so its seeds travel.
The lotus leaf's waxy bumps, which make rain roll off and wash it clean.
The termite mound's thick walls, which slow down the heat getting in.

flow.do: Help your child draw the invention and label each part. Next to it, they write what they copied and how they will test it.
flow.say: Draw your invention and label every part. Then write one sentence: the idea I copied is... And one more: I will test it by...
flow.kid: Draw your invention. Label each part. Write what you copied. Write how you will test it.

flow.do: Day 2. Build a rough prototype from home materials. Don't make it perfect. Make it good enough to test.
flow.say: A prototype is a quick, rough first try. Engineers expect it to have problems. That's how they learn.
flow.kid: Build a rough first version. It doesn't need to be pretty. It needs to be good enough to test.

flow.do: Test the prototype fairly against the plain version, changing only one thing. Measure something real. Count coins held or drops rolled off. Or time the ice, or measure a slope's height.
flow.say: Let's test it against the plain version. What will you measure? Change only one thing, and test each 3 times.
flow.kid: Test your invention against the plain version. Measure something real. Test each one 3 times. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Tests that work at home. A grip invention: count coins in a bag before it slips, or lift a board until it slides and measure the height. A clean or dry invention: drip 5 drops and count how many roll off. A cool invention: put an ice cube inside and time it in the sun.

check.q: You test your grip pad against a plain pad. Which test is fair?
options: Same weight, same slope and same surface, only the pad changes
The grip pad on a rough floor and the plain pad on a smooth floor
Test only your grip pad, many times
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes, here the pad. Then any difference must come from the pad. Testing on two different floors changes two things, so you can't tell which one mattered. Testing only your own pad gives nothing to compare it with.

flow.do: Day 3. Look at the results. Change one thing to make the invention better, and test again.
flow.say: What went wrong, or what could be better? Change one thing, then test again. Did it improve?
flow.kid: What could be better? Change one thing. Test it again. Did the numbers get better?

chart.title: Made-up example: a burr-hook bag strap, before and after improving
chart.y: Coins held before the strap slipped
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a results chart can look like.

flow.do: Make an invention poster: its name, the problem, the living thing and its design, a drawing, and the before and after numbers. Show it to the family.
flow.say: Give your invention a name. Then tell the family about it, like a real inventor. Don't forget to give credit to the living thing that taught you.
flow.kid: Name your invention. Make a poster. Show your family. Say which living thing gave you the idea!
flow.think: Your invention borrowed an idea from a living thing. Is there anything you could do for that plant or animal in return?

challenges.title: Make a Fastener Like a Burr
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You copy the burr's design, tiny hooks catching in loops, to make your own fastener from paperclips, and test how many coins it can hold.
challenges.problem: Make a fastener that joins a piece of towel to a cardboard strip, using hooks like a burr. It must open and close again and again, and hold as many coins as possible.
constraints: No glue, no knots and no tape on the towel side.
The fastener must open and close 10 times and still work.
Measure what it holds by adding coins, one at a time, to a small bag hanging from the towel.
materials: a cardboard strip about as long as your hand, and sticky tape
a small piece of old towel, about the size of your palm, and a piece of smooth cotton cloth
a small plastic bag, a clothes peg and 20 or more coins of the same kind
general: Bend each paperclip so one end makes a small, tight hook, like a letter J. Small hooks catch more loops.
Tape the hooks in rows on the cardboard, all pointing the same way and sticking up.
Use more hooks to hold more. Each hook holds a little, and the little holds add up.
creative: Point half the hooks one way and half the other way, so the towel cannot slide off in either direction.
Real Velcro has hundreds of hooks in a small space. Try making your hooks smaller and closer together.
Some fasteners use tiny mushroom shapes on both sides that snap into each other. Could you make one with no loops at all?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own fastener copied from nature. Draw it, build it and test it with coins. Does it beat your paperclip version?

flow.do: 1. Unbend each paperclip partly, so it has a straight leg and a small hook at one end, like a J. 2. Tape the straight legs flat onto the cardboard strip, with the hooks sticking up and all pointing the same way. Start with 4 hooks.
flow.say: Each paperclip becomes one hook of a burr. Make the hooks small and tight, and all point them the same way.
flow.kid: Bend each paperclip into a J shape. Tape 4 of them on the cardboard. Hooks up, all pointing the same way.
flow.parent: Paperclip ends can be sharp. Bend them with fingers, or with pliers held by a grown-up. Point the hook tips away from fingers. Smaller hooks catch towel loops better.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Fastener Like a Burr. You bend paperclips into tiny hooks and tape them to a strip of card.

flow.do: 1. Press the towel onto the hooks and slide it a little in the direction the hooks point, so they catch. 2. Hold the cardboard upright, with the towel hanging from it. 3. Clip the plastic bag to the bottom of the towel with the peg. 4. Add coins one at a time until the towel pulls off. 5. Write the number.
flow.say: Let's see how strong four hooks are. Add the coins one by one, gently. Count until it falls.
flow.kid: Hook the towel on. Hang the bag from the towel. Add coins one at a time. Count until it falls!

ask.q: What happens if you try smooth cotton instead of towel?
good: It hardly holds, because there are no loops to catch.
The hooks slide off the smooth cloth.

flow.do: 1. Add 4 more hooks, to make 8. 2. Test again with coins. 3. Try the smooth cotton cloth too. 4. Open and close the fastener 10 times, and test once more.
flow.say: Double the hooks. Do you think it will hold double the coins? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Add 4 more hooks and test again. Does it hold more coins? Now try smooth cotton. What happens?

check.q: With 4 hooks the towel held 6 coins. With 8 hooks it held about 12. What does this show?
options: Each hook holds a little, and the holds add up
Hooks don't matter, only the towel matters
The coins got lighter
check.why: Each hook catches a few loops and holds a little weight. Doubling the hooks roughly doubles the holding. Real Velcro has hundreds of tiny hooks, so it holds a lot. Picking 'only the towel matters' misses that the same towel held more when there were more hooks.

flow.parent: Expect the towel to hold a few coins with 4 hooks and more with 8. The smooth cotton usually falls off at once. Results wobble, so test twice if you have time.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent one improvement and test it.
flow.say: Here are the ways engineers usually make hooks hold better, and some creative ideas. Can you invent a better one?
flow.kid: Read the usual ways and the creative ideas. Pick one, or invent your own. Test it with coins!
flow.think: George de Mestral spent about ten years getting his hooks just right. Why do you think it took so long?

challenges.title: The Rain-Proof Name Tag
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the lotus effect. You design a name tag for a school bag or a plant pot that stays clean and readable when it is dusty and wet.
challenges.problem: Design a paper name tag that stays clean and readable when dust and rain land on it. Copy the lotus leaf's design.
constraints: It must start as ordinary paper.
Your name must still be readable at the end.
Test it fairly: the same pinch of dust and the same 10 sprinkles of water on every tag.
materials: 4 small squares of paper and a pencil
a candle (not lit), and wax crayons
a pinch of chalk dust or dry soil
general: Rub candle wax thickly all over the tag. Water will bead up and roll off.
Colour the tag hard all over with wax crayons, pressing firmly.
Cover the tag with clear sticky tape, so water can't soak in.
creative: Crumple the paper and flatten it before waxing, to give it tiny bumps like a lotus leaf.
Ask a grown-up to make a sooty Lotus Spoon, and compare how drops roll on it and on your tag.
Use a real chembu leaf as the tag, and scratch your name into it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own rain-proof tag. Draw it, make it, and test it against the plain paper tag.

flow.do: 1. Write your name in pencil on 4 paper squares. 2. Leave one plain. 3. Rub one hard all over with the candle, front and edges. 4. Colour one hard all over with wax crayons. 5. Cover one with clear sticky tape.
flow.say: We're making four tags. One plain, one waxed with a candle, one crayoned, one taped. Which do you think will stay cleanest?
flow.kid: Write your name on 4 paper squares. Leave one plain. Wax one with the candle. Crayon one, and tape one.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Rain-Proof Name Tag. You make four name tags, each with a different coating.

flow.do: 1. Lean the tags on a book, tilted. 2. Sprinkle the same thin pinch of dust on each. 3. Dip your fingers in water and flick 10 sprinkles onto each tag. 4. Wait 1 minute and look.
flow.say: Same dust, same water, same tilt for every tag. That makes it fair. Now watch what the drops do.
flow.kid: Tilt the tags on a book. Sprinkle a little dust on each. Flick 10 sprinkles of water. Watch the drops!

ask.q: On which tag did the drops roll off and take the dust?
good: The candle-waxed one.
The crayon one, a bit.

flow.parent: The plain tag soaks up the water and the dust becomes a muddy smudge. The candle-waxed tag makes the water bead up and roll, carrying some dust away. Crayon works a little less well. On the taped tag, drops often stick and leave dirty spots when they dry.

flow.do: Compare the tags. Then read the usual solutions and the creative ideas, and try one improvement.
flow.say: Which tag would you trust on a school bag in the monsoon? Can you make it even better?
flow.kid: Which tag is cleanest? Try one idea to make it even better. Test it the same way.

check.q: Why did the candle-waxed tag stay cleaner than the taped tag?
options: Water rolled off the wax in balls and carried dust away
Wax is a darker colour
The tape was too sticky
check.why: Wax hardly pulls on water, so drops stay round and roll off, picking up dust as they go. That is part of how a lotus leaf stays clean. Smooth tape lets drops sit flat and stay, so the dust dries in spots. Picking 'too sticky' is a fair guess, but the tape's outside is not sticky.

flow.do: Make a final tag with your best idea and tie it on a school bag or a plant pot. Check it after the next rain.
flow.say: Real inventions get tested in the real world. Let's check your tag after the next rain.
flow.kid: Make your best tag. Put it on your bag or a plant pot. Check it after it rains!
flow.think: The lotus leaf uses wax and tiny bumps. Your tag only has wax. What could give it bumps?
