opts: Making machines that look like animals
Copying how a living thing solves a problem, to solve a human problem
quiz.why: Biomimicry copies how living things solve the problems of their own lives. Picking 'machines that look like animals' is a common mix-up. A good copy takes how it works, not how it looks.

quiz.p: Which of these is an example of biomimicry?
opts: Velcro, copied from a burr's hooks
A toy shaped like a fish
quiz.why: Velcro copies a working design, the hooks. The plastic flower and the fish toy only copy a look. A photo copies nothing that works.

quiz.p: Why does a burdock plant have hooked burrs?
opts: So animals carry their seeds to new ground
So they can climb up walls
quiz.why: Seeds that fall under the parent plant must share their parent's light, water and soil. Hooks catch in fur, so animals carry the seeds far away. Picking 'so animals cannot eat them' is a fair guess, because spines often protect plants. But the burdock's hooks catch and hold on, which is what a seed needs to ride away.

quiz.p: Why do burrs stick to woollen socks better than to smooth socks?
opts: Their hooks catch in the wool's loops
quiz.why: Hooks need loops to catch. Wool and fur are full of loops. Smooth cloth has none. Picking 'wool is sticky' means thinking the grip is glue. It is hooks and loops.
quiz.context: In the Sock Walk, you walked through weeds with a fluffy sock on one shoe and a smooth sock on the other.

quiz.p: Velcro's hooks hold tight when you press the two strips together. Why can you still peel them apart easily?
opts: The hooks melt when you pull
Peeling pulls only a few bendy hooks at a time, and each one bends open and slips out of its loop
Velcro has glue that dries out
quiz.why: Peeling makes only a few hooks let go at once, so each pull is small. Pulling the whole strip straight off is much harder, because every hook must let go together. Burrs come off fur the same way, a few hooks at a time. Picking 'glue' means thinking the grip is sticky. It is hooks and loops.

quiz.p: Why does a lotus plant need their leaves to stay clean?
opts: So people think it looks pretty
So frogs can sit on it
Dirt would block the sunlight the leaf uses to make food
quiz.why: A leaf makes food from sunlight, so dirt on it means less food. Germs and spores left on a leaf can also make the plant sick. Picking 'so people think it looks pretty' looks at the lotus from our side. The lotus keeps clean for their own life.

quiz.p: What makes a lotus leaf stay clean?
opts: Tiny waxy bumps that make water roll off and carry dirt away
It is sticky, so dirt can't land
quiz.why: The bumps and wax make drops stay round and roll, picking up dirt. Picking 'perfectly smooth' is the most common wrong idea. The leaf is bumpy.

quiz.p: On which surface did the drops roll off most easily in the leaf experiment?
quiz.why: On the chembu leaf, drops stay round and roll at a small tilt. Paper soaks water up. On steel, drops sit as domes and often stay put. Picking steel usually means thinking 'smooth and shiny means slippery for water'.
quiz.context: In the leaf experiment, you dripped 5 drops on each surface and tilted them on a book.

chart.title: Made-up example results: drops that rolled off at the tilt (out of 5)

quiz.p: Why did the bullet train get a long, beak-shaped nose?
opts: So it looked like a bird
So it could carry more people
So it pushed the air aside slowly and came out of tunnels without a loud boom
quiz.why: A blunt nose squeezes the air in a tunnel, which bursts out with a boom. A long nose that widens slowly parts the air gently, like a kingfisher's beak parts water. Picking 'so it looked like a bird' mixes up copying the look with copying the design.

quiz.p: How does a gecko stick to a glass window?
opts: Millions of tiny hairs get so close that their atoms pull on the glass
Tiny claws that dig into the glass
quiz.why: Gecko hairs split into hundreds of millions of tiny tips. They get extremely close to the glass, and the atoms pull on each other. Picking 'claws dig in' doesn't work on glass, which is too hard to dig into. There is no glue, and experiments ruled out suction.

quiz.p: In the ice experiment, why did the cup wrapped in thick newspaper keep its ice longer than the bare cup?
opts: Thick walls slow down the heat getting in
The newspaper cup had a bigger ice cube
quiz.why: Heat from the sun is always trying to get in. Thick walls slow it down. Picking 'newspaper is cold' is a common idea. Walls don't make cold. They slow the heat getting in. A bigger ice cube would make it an unfair test.
quiz.context: In the ice experiment, you put the same size of ice cube in cups with different walls and left them in the sun.

quiz.p: What do scientists now think moves the air inside termite mounds near Bengaluru?
opts: The walls warming in the day and cooling at night
quiz.why: A 2015 study found the walls warm and cool faster than the middle, which moves the air one way by day and the other way by night. There are no fans. Picking 'the air never moves' would mean the termites run out of fresh air.

quiz.p: You test your grip invention. Which is a fair test?
opts: Test it and a plain version on the same slope, with the same weight
Test your invention on a rough floor, and the plain version on a smooth floor
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the floors are different, you can't tell whether the invention or the floor made the difference. Testing only your invention gives nothing to compare it with.

quiz.p: Look at the made-up splash results. Which shape splashed least?
quiz.why: The shortest bar is the pointed beak, with 2 splash spots. Picking 'flat pancake' means reading the tallest bar as the best. Here a tall bar means a big splash.
quiz.context: In the splash experiment, you dropped three dough shapes of the same weight into a bucket and counted the splash spots on the newspaper around it.

chart.title: Made-up results: splash spots on the newspaper

quiz.p: Where did the burr's hooks and the gecko's hairs come from?
opts: They were made in a factory
quiz.why: Over many generations, plants with better hooks and geckos with better grip left more young. So those features spread. Picking 'a scientist designed them' mixes up nature's designs with people's copies of them.

quiz.p: Deep down, the gecko's grip and the water drop's round shape both come from…
opts: Electric pulls between atoms and molecules
quiz.why: Gecko hair tips and the wall pull on each other with tiny electric forces. Water molecules pull on each other with electric forces too, which rounds a drop. Picking gravity is common, but gravity here is far too weak.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether a thin film of water helps geckos grip
quiz.why: Scientists agree the pull between atoms does most of the gecko's grip. They still argue about how much a thin film of water helps. The other three can be seen with a microscope or your own eyes.

applications: Velcro, hook and loop, on shoes, bags, watch straps, jackets and blood pressure cuffs.
Self-cleaning outside paint, glass and roof tiles that copy the lotus leaf.
Water-repelling raincoats, umbrellas and school bag fabrics.
The long, beak-like noses of high-speed trains.
Quieter fans and train parts with soft, fringed edges, like owl feathers.
Gecko-style grippers on robots, and tests of grippers for catching things in space.
Buildings with thick walls and night-time air channels that need less air conditioning.
Light, strong honeycomb panels inside aeroplanes and doors.
Wind turbine and fan blades with bumpy front edges, copied from humpback whale flippers.
Super-slippery coatings, copied from the pitcher plant, so sticky things slide out of pipes and bottles.
Fog-catching nets that collect drinking water on dry hills.
Grippy shoe soles with grooves that let water out, like tree frog toe pads.
Swimming goggles, gliders and aeroplane wings shaped after birds and fish.
Hospitals testing gecko-inspired dry tapes that hold without glue and peel off gently.
Traditional thick-walled mud houses and earthen water pots that stay cool in Indian summers.

open_questions.q: Exactly how much does a thin film of water help a gecko grip?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree the pull between atoms does most of the work. Experiments disagree on how much damp air adds.

open_questions.q: How exactly do termite mounds move their air?
open_questions.why_open: Different kinds of termite build different mounds. Day and night warming, wind and the termites themselves may all play a part, in different mixes.

open_questions.q: Can we make gecko tape that works as well as a gecko, for years?
open_questions.why_open: Copies grip well at first, but get dirty or worn. Real gecko feet clean themselves and grow new hairs when the gecko sheds their skin.

open_questions.q: How many of nature's designs have we not even noticed yet?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have described only a small part of the kinds of living things on Earth. Most have never been studied closely.

open_questions.q: Can we build an 'artificial leaf' that makes fuel from sunlight, as well as plants make food?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made small ones that work in the lab. Nobody has yet made one cheap and long-lasting enough to use everywhere.

open_questions.q: Can we make self-cleaning surfaces that last?
open_questions.why_open: The lotus grows new wax all the time. Man-made copies wear off with rubbing, and scientists are still looking for tougher ones.

open_questions.q: Should a company be able to patent a design copied from a plant or an animal?
open_questions.why_open: This is a question of fairness, not only science. Countries and people still disagree.

open_questions.q: Are there designs that only living things can make, or that only people can make?
open_questions.why_open: Living things build at ordinary temperatures with water and sunlight. People can use fire, metal and electricity. Where the limits are, nobody knows.

maths.problem: After the Sock Walk, 18 seeds were stuck to the fluffy sock and 3 to the smooth sock. Look at the chart. How many times more seeds did the fluffy sock collect?
maths.explain: The fluffy sock collected 18 seeds. The smooth sock collected 3. 18 divided by 3 is 6. So the fluffy sock collected 6 times as many. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 18.
maths.context: This is about the Sock Walk. You walked through weeds with a fluffy sock over one shoe and a smooth sock over the other, then counted the hitchhiker seeds on each.

chart.title: Made-up example: seeds that rode home on each sock

maths.why_maths: Saying 'more seeds' is a start. Dividing tells us exactly how much better loops are than smooth cloth at catching hooks.

maths.problem: In the fastener challenge, 4 paperclip hooks held 6 coins. If every hook holds the same, how many coins would 8 hooks hold? And 12 hooks?
maths.answer: 8 hooks hold about 12 coins. 12 hooks hold about 18 coins.
maths.explain: 8 hooks is 2 lots of 4 hooks, so it holds 2 lots of 6 coins. 2 times 6 is 12. 12 hooks is 3 lots of 4 hooks. 3 times 6 is 18. Real tests wobble a little, so your numbers may be close to these, not exactly the same.
maths.context: This is about the fastener challenge. You bent paperclips into hooks, hooked a towel onto them, and added coins in a bag until the towel fell.

answer_chart.title: Hooks and coins held, if each hook holds the same

maths.why_maths: Each hook holds a little, and the holds add up. Multiplying lets you predict how many hooks you need before you build.

maths.problem: In the ice experiment, the ice in the bare cup was gone after 25 minutes. The ice in the newspaper cup lasted 50 minutes. How many minutes longer did the newspaper cup keep its ice?
maths.explain: 50 minutes take away 25 minutes is 25 minutes. So the thick newspaper walls kept the ice for 25 minutes longer. That is twice as long as the bare cup, because 25 + 25 = 50.
maths.context: This is about the ice experiment. You put ice cubes of the same size into cups with different walls, left them in the sun, and timed how long each lasted.

answer_chart.title: Made-up example: minutes until the ice was gone

maths.why_maths: Taking one time from another tells us exactly how much the thick walls helped, in minutes we can understand.

maths.problem: In the splash experiment, the pancake made 22, 18 and 25 splash spots in three tries. The beak made 2, 0 and 3. Find the middle value for each. Then draw a bar chart.
maths.answer: The pancake's middle value is 22. The beak's middle value is 2. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Put each set of numbers in order, smallest first. Pancake: 18, 22, 25. The middle one is 22. Beak: 0, 2, 3. The middle one is 2. Draw one bar for each shape, as tall as its middle value. The pancake's bar is 11 times as tall as the beak's, because 2 times 11 is 22.
maths.context: This is about the splash experiment. You dropped dough shapes of the same weight into a bucket and counted the wet spots that splashes left on the newspaper.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. Taking the middle of three tries, then drawing bars, shows the real difference between the shapes at a glance.

maths.problem: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, did the leaf experiment with 8 drops on each surface. She tilted the steel plate, and 4 drops rolled off. On the chembu leaf, all 8 rolled off. What fraction of the drops rolled off the steel plate?
maths.explain: 4 out of 8 drops rolled off. 4 is half of 8, because 4 + 4 = 8. So half the drops rolled off the steel. On the leaf, 8 out of 8 rolled off, which is all of them, the whole.
maths.context: This is about the leaf experiment. You put drops of water on a lotus-like leaf and a steel plate, tilted them on a book, and counted the drops that rolled off.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let us compare surfaces fairly, even if we put a different number of drops on each.

roots.context: We have been learning how burdock plants, lotus leaves, kingfishers, geckos and termites solve problems in their own lives, and how people copied them. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: On the chembu leaf, your drops rolled into balls and carried the dust away. The leaf needs this, because dirt would block its sunlight and germs could make it sick. Plants like chembu found this answer over many generations, long before people made self-cleaning paint. So the first inventors on Earth were living things solving their own problems.
deep_truth.habit: We think of inventing as something only people do, in workshops and labs. But the chembu leaf, the burdock and the kingfisher each solved a problem in their own lives long before any person copied them.
deep_truth.evidence: Drops roll off a chembu leaf and take the dust with them, while paper soaks them up. Self-cleaning wall paint, first sold in the late 1990s, copies the same tiny waxy bumps.

three.who_am_i: Your hands and your brain were shaped over many generations too. When you invent, you do what living things have always done: solve the problems of your life.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing is solving problems all the time: spreading their seeds, keeping clean, catching food, keeping cool.
three.what_is_this_world: Water, air and heat follow the same rules for every living thing and every machine. That is why a bird's answer can work for a train.

roots.thread: The burdock, the lotus and the kingfisher each solved a different problem. Yet they all worked with the same few rules: water pulling on itself more than on wax, water pushing back on a beak, a hook holding in a loop. From one set of rules for the whole world came countless different answers, one in each kind of living thing. A person who copies a burr is one living thing learning from another, and the idea passes from plant to person.

teachings.teaching: A person who works without clinging, offering the work to something greater, is not stained by wrong, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
teachings.link: The Gita used the lotus leaf as its picture long before microscopes showed why water rolls off it. The leaf lives on the pond, yet the water does not wet it, and the mud does not stay on it.

teachings.teaching: People follow the ways of the Earth. The Earth follows the ways of Heaven. Heaven follows the Tao, the Way. The Way follows what is natural.
teachings.link: Biomimicry is people learning from the ways of the Earth, quite literally: an engineer watching a kingfisher to learn how to build a train.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree inside it. Nothing exists all by itself.
teachings.link: Look deeply at a Velcro strap and you can see the burdock plant, the dog that carried their burrs, and the engineer who looked closely. The invention is made of all of them.

science.text: Life on Earth has been changing for about 3.8 billion years. Every living design today comes from a long line of living things that survived. This is evolution.
Animals that are not related often evolve the same shape when they face the same problem. Scientists call this convergent evolution.

other_view.view: Many biologists and engineers say evolution has no plan and no goal. In their view, a burr did not invent anything: seeds with better hooks simply travelled further. People plan, imagine and choose, so human invention is something new and different. That is an honest view.

practice.title: Watch one drop
practice.say: Let's take a lotus or chembu leaf, or the sooty spoon, or a candle-waxed paper. I'll put one drop of water on it. Hold it very still. Breathe in slowly. Now tilt it, just a little, and breathe out slowly as the drop rolls. Watch it go all the way. Look at the leaf. Is it wet? Let's do it once more, in silence.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought they knew how termite mounds stay fresh inside. In 1961, a Swiss scientist, Martin Lüscher, wrote about mounds in Africa. He said the warmth of millions of termites and their fungus garden heats the air in the middle. The warm air rises up a central chimney, like smoke, and pulls fresh air in from below. Books repeated this for decades, and an architect copied the idea for a building in Zimbabwe. But nobody had measured the air inside a living mound through a whole day and night. In 2015, Hunter King, Samuel Ocko and L. Mahadevan of Harvard University did. They put tiny sensors into mounds of the termite Odontotermes obesus near Bengaluru. By day, the sun warmed the thin outer ridges of the mound faster than its thick middle, and the air moved one way. At night, the outer ridges cooled first, and the air moved the other way. The termites' own warmth was not what drove the air. The mound breathes with the day and the night.
how_we_found_out.who: Martin Lüscher (the old idea), and Hunter King, Samuel Ocko and L. Mahadevan (the measurements near Bengaluru)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The termites' own warmth heats the air, which rises up a chimney and pulls fresh air in. Sensors in real mounds near Bengaluru showed that the sun's warming by day and the cooling at night move the air instead.
